2. 'Processing' is any treatment that subjects a commodity to a change, even without
creating a new commodity.
3. Blending different grades of ore constitutes processing, not manufacturing.

cases.title: Jindal Stainless Ltd. v. State of Haryana
cases.facts:
Various State Governments enacted laws levying an 'Entry Tax' on goods entering their local
areas for consumption, use, or sale. Hundreds of companies challenged these entry taxes
across India, arguing that they violated Article 301 of the Constitution, which guarantees the
freedom of trade, commerce, and intercourse throughout the territory of India. The States
argued that the tax was valid under Entry 52 of List II and was 'compensatory' in nature.
cases.issues:
1. Does a State's Entry Tax inherently violate the freedom of trade and commerce under
Article 301?
2. What is the scope of 'compensatory taxes' in relation to Article 301?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The companies relied on the Atiabari and Automobile Transport precedents, arguing that
any tax acting as a direct physical barrier on the movement of goods restricts free trade. A tax
can only survive if it is strictly 'compensatory' (i.e., the state provides a direct, measurable
facility like a road in return for the tax).
B. Defendant / Revenue / State
The States argued that the power of taxation is a sovereign power under List II. Article 301
cannot completely strip states of their right to generate revenue to build infrastructure.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: A 9-Judge Constitution Bench upheld the constitutional validity of Entry Tax,
overruling previous strict tests for compensatory taxes.
cases.reasoning:
The Court fundamentally reshaped Indian federal taxation principles. It held that the power
to tax is a sovereign attribute of the States. Article 301 guarantees free trade but does not
mean trade must be tax-free. A non-discriminatory tax on goods is not an unconstitutional
restriction on free trade. The Court rejected the strict mathematical test for 'compensatory
taxes' established in earlier cases. It held that states do not need to prove a direct, measurable
quid pro quo (like building a specific road) to validate an entry tax. As long as the tax is non-
discriminatory (treating out-of-state goods and local goods equally), it is constitutionally valid.
This restored massive revenue-generating powers to the States.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. A non-discriminatory tax on goods does not inherently violate the freedom of trade
under Article 301.
2. The strict mathematical 'quid pro quo' requirement for compensatory taxes is
discarded.
3. States have the sovereign power to levy Entry Tax provided it does not discriminate
against imported goods.

cases.title: CIT v. Woodward Governor India P. Ltd.
cases.facts:
The assessee company had taken a loan in foreign currency for revenue purposes. Due to
fluctuations in the foreign exchange rate, the liability of the company increased significantly
at the end of the financial year . The company followed the mercantile system of accounting. It
claimed this 'unrealized' foreign exchange fluctuation loss as a deductible business
expenditure under Section 37(1) of the ITA, even though the loan had not yet been fully
repaid.
cases.issues:
1. Can an unrealized foreign exchange fluctuation loss, recorded at the end of the year
under the mercantile system, be claimed as a deductible revenue expenditure under
Section 37(1)?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The Revenue argued that the loss was purely notional and contingent. Since the actual
payment had not been made, no real loss had crystallized. Allowing a deduction for a
hypothetical loss violates accounting principles.
B. Defendant / Revenue / State
The assessee argued that under the mercantile system (and Accounting Standard 11),
liabilities must be revalued on the balance sheet date. The increased liability is a certainty,
not a contingency, and is an accrued business loss.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the assessee, allowing the deduction for the
foreign exchange fluctuation loss.
cases.reasoning:
The Court aligned tax law with standard accounting practices. It held that when an assessee
follows the mercantile system of accounting, liabilities must be recorded when they accrue,
not when they are actually paid. The foreign currency loan was taken for revenue purposes.
The fluctuation in the exchange rate is a reality of the market. On the last day of the
accounting year , the company is legally required to revalue its outstanding liabilities. The
increased liability due to exchange rate changes is an accrued, certain liability, not a
contingent one. Therefore, the loss represents an accrued expenditure wholly and exclusively
laid out for business purposes, making it fully deductible under Section 37(1).
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Unrealized foreign exchange fluctuation losses on revenue account are deductible
business expenditures under Section 37(1).
2. Under the mercantile system, liabilities are deductible when they accrue, not upon
actual payment.
3. Tax computation must generally respect mandatory Accounting Standards (like AS-11).

cases.title: Honda Siel Power Products Ltd. v. CIT
cases.facts:
The Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT) passed an order against Honda Siel. While passing
the order , the Tribunal completely failed to consider a binding judgment of the jurisdictional
High Court that the assessee had cited during the hearing. The assessee filed a rectification
application under Section 254(2) of the ITA, pointing out that ignoring a binding precedent is
a 'mistake apparent from the record'. The ITAT admitted the mistake and recalled its order .
The Revenue challenged the ITAT's power to recall its own order .
cases.issues:
1. Does the failure of the Tribunal to consider a binding judicial precedent constitute a
'mistake apparent from the record' under Section 254(2)?
2. Does the ITAT have the power to recall its order to rectify such a mistake?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The Revenue argued that Section 254(2) only allows the rectification of minor clerical or
arithmetic errors. Recalling an entire order amounts to 'reviewing' the judgment, a power the
ITAT does not possess.
B. Defendant / Revenue / State
The assessee argued that ignoring a binding High Court judgment is an egregious error of law
apparent on the record. If the Tribunal cannot rectify this, the assessee is forced into
unnecessary appeals.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the assessee, upholding the ITAT's power to
rectify the mistake and recall the order .
cases.reasoning:
The Court clarified the scope of Section 254(2). The purpose of the section is to ensure that a
mistake made by the Tribunal does not cause prejudice to the taxpayer . The Court held that a
binding decision of the Supreme Court or the jurisdictional High Court is the law of the land.
If a Tribunal fails to consider a binding precedent cited before it, it commits an error of law
that is 'apparent from the record'. To rectify this mistake, the Tribunal has the inherent power
to recall its order and hear the matter afresh. This is not a 'review' of the merits based on new
arguments, but a correction of an institutional error to uphold the rule of law.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. The failure of a Tribunal to consider a binding precedent constitutes a 'mistake
apparent from the record'.
2. The ITAT can invoke Section 254(2) to recall its order to rectify such a legal error .
3. The power of rectification exists to ensure that no party suffers due to a mistake
committed by the court/tribunal.

cases.title: Associated Cement Companies Ltd. v. Commissioner of Customs
cases.facts:
The assessee imported drawings, designs, technical manuals, and engineering data from a
foreign collaborator as part of a technology transfer agreement. The customs authorities
assessed these documents as 'goods' and sought to levy customs duty not just on the value of
the paper they were printed on, but on the massive intellectual value of the technical know-
how contained within them. The assessee argued that intellectual property is intangible and
cannot be subjected to customs duty as 'goods'.
cases.issues:
1. Are drawings, designs, and manuals imported on paper classified as tangible 'goods'
subject to customs duty?
2. Should the customs valuation include the value of the intangible intellectual property
(know-how) contained within the physical medium?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The assessee argued that they were paying royalties for the transfer of technology and ideas,
which are invisible and intangible. The paper manuals were just a medium. Customs duty can
only be levied on physical goods.
B. Defendant / Revenue / State
The Revenue argued that once ideas are put on paper and imported, the paper becomes a
specialized commodity with immense value. The value of the intellectual content cannot be
separated from the physical carrier .
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Revenue, holding that intellectual property
put on a physical medium constitutes 'goods' and is fully dutiable.
cases.reasoning:
Foreshadowing the logic in the TCS software case, the Court held that the definition of
'goods' in the Customs Act is extremely wide. While technical know-how is intangible, the
moment it is manifested on a physical medium (like drawings, blueprints, or diskettes) and
imported across the border , it becomes a tangible article. The Court held that customs
valuation must be based on the true transaction value of the imported item. The value of a
technical manual is not the cost of the blank paper , but the value of the engineering data it
contains. Therefore, the intellectual value is inextricably linked to the physical medium, and
customs duty is payable on the entire combined value.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Technical know-how, designs, and software put on a physical medium and imported
are tangible 'goods'.
2. Customs duty is levied on the entire value of the imported item, including its
intellectual content.
3. Intellectual property cannot be artificially separated from its physical carrier for
valuation purposes.

cases.title: Tuticorin Alkali Chemicals & Fertilizers Ltd. v. CIT
cases.facts:
A company was in the process of setting up its manufacturing plant and had not yet
commenced business operations. It had borrowed huge term loans from banks for
construction. Since the funds were not immediately required, the company invested the
surplus borrowed funds in short-term bank deposits and earned interest on them. The
company sought to set off this interest income against the massive interest expenditure it was
paying on the loans, essentially capitalizing the income to reduce project costs.
cases.issues:
1. Is interest earned on surplus borrowed funds prior to the commencement of business
taxable as 'Income from Other Sources'?
2. Can this pre-commencement interest income be set off against the interest paid on the
borrowed loans?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The assessee argued that the interest income was inextricably linked to the borrowing for the
plant. According to accounting practices, this income should be adjusted against the project
cost (capitalized) rather than taxed as revenue income.
B. Defendant / Revenue / State
The Revenue argued that income from bank deposits is a distinct, independent source of
revenue. Since the business had not commenced, it cannot be classified as business income or
set off against capital expenditure.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Revenue, holding that the interest earned is
fully taxable under 'Income from Other Sources'.
cases.reasoning:
The Court separated tax law from general accounting practices. It held that under the Income
Tax Act, if a company earns interest from bank deposits, it falls squarely under the head
'Income from Other Sources' (Section 56). The fact that the business has not yet commenced is
irrelevant; the income has accrued. The Court firmly rejected the argument for a set-off. The
interest paid on the loans is a capital expenditure (since the business hasn't started), while the
interest earned is a revenue receipt. Tax law does not permit setting off revenue income
against capital expenditure. Therefore, the interest earned must be taxed independently.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Interest earned on short-term deposits of borrowed funds before the commencement
of business is taxable as 'Income from Other Sources'.
2. Such revenue income cannot be set off against the capital expenditure of interest paid
on the loans.
3. Accounting principles (capitalizing pre-operative income) do not override strict
statutory heads of income in tax law.

cases.title: CIT v. Podar Cement Pvt. Ltd.
cases.facts:
Podar Cement purchased a block of flats, paid the full consideration, and took physical
possession. They let out the flats and received rental income. However , the formal legal sale
deed was not registered in their name due to administrative delays. The Revenue sought to
tax the rental income under the head 'Income from House Property' (Section 22). The assessee
argued that under the Transfer of Property Act, legal ownership does not pass without a
registered sale deed. Therefore, they were not the legal 'owners' of the property and could not
be taxed under Section 22.
cases.issues:
1. Who is the 'owner' of house property for the purpose of taxation under Section 22 of
the ITA?
2. Does taxation require strict legal ownership (a registered sale deed), or is equitable
ownership/possession sufficient?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The assessee relied on strict civil law, arguing that Section 22 explicitly taxes the 'owner'.
Without a registered conveyance deed, they were merely possessors, and the income should
be taxed as business income or other sources.
B. Defendant / Revenue / State
The Revenue argued that tax law must reflect economic reality. The assessee paid the money,
possessed the property, and enjoyed the rental income as if they were the owner . They must
be taxed as the owner .
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Revenue, interpreting 'owner' broadly to
include the person in actual possession enjoying the fruits of the property.
cases.reasoning:
The Court revolutionized the concept of ownership in tax law. It held that the strict, technical
definition of 'owner' under the Transfer of Property Act does not apply rigidly to the Income
Tax Act. The objective of Section 22 is to tax the income derived from the property. The Court
defined 'owner' for tax purposes as the person who is entitled to receive the income from the
property in their own right. If a person pays full consideration, takes possession, exercises
total control, and receives rent, they are the 'owner' under Section 22, regardless of whether
the formal registration of the sale deed is pending. To hold otherwise would allow massive
tax evasion.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. The term 'owner' under Section 22 (Income from House Property) is not strictly
confined to the registered legal owner .
2. 'Owner' includes a person who takes possession, exercises control, and receives rental
income in their own right.
3. Tax law interprets ownership based on economic reality and the enjoyment of the
property's fruits.

cases.title: Union of India v. Dharamendra Textile Processors
cases.facts:
Under Section 11AC of the Central Excise Act, a penalty equal to 100% of the evaded duty is
imposed if a manufacturer evades duty by reason of fraud, collusion, or willful misstatement.
Several manufacturers who were caught evading duty argued that penalty provisions are
quasi-criminal. Therefore, they argued that the Adjudicating Authority must establish mens
rea (criminal/guilty intent) and has the discretion to reduce the penalty below 100% if the
facts are mitigating.
cases.issues:
1. Is mens rea an essential ingredient for imposing a civil penalty under tax statutes
like Section 11AC of the Excise Act?
2. Does the authority have discretion to reduce the penalty amount below the statutorily
prescribed 100%?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The assessees argued that penalty is a punishment. The word 'penalty' implies discretion. The
authorities should be allowed to reduce the penalty to 10% or 20% depending on the severity
of the intent.
B. Defendant / Revenue / State
The Revenue argued that Section 11AC is a civil liability mechanism for protecting revenue,
not a criminal statute. The word 'shall' in the section makes the 100% penalty mandatory
upon proof of evasion.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: A 3-Judge Bench of the Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Revenue, holding that the
penalty under Section 11AC is mandatory and does not require strict mens rea.
cases.reasoning:
The Court clarified the nature of tax penalties. A penalty imposed for tax evasion is a civil
liability intended to compensate the state for revenue loss and ensure strict statutory
compliance. It is not a criminal punishment. Therefore, the strict criminal law concept of
mens rea does not apply to civil tax penalties unless the statute explicitly demands it.
Furthermore, the Court interpreted the language of Section 11AC. The section states the
evader 'shall be liable to a penalty equal to the duty so determined'. The Court ruled that
'shall' means mandatory. Once the authority establishes that duty was evaded through fraud
or suppression, it has absolutely no discretion to reduce the penalty below the prescribed
100%.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Civil penalties in tax statutes do not require strict proof of mens rea (criminal intent)
unless specified.
2. The penalty under Section 11AC of the Central Excise Act is mandatory.
3. Adjudicating authorities have no discretionary power to reduce the statutory 100%
penalty for duty evasion.

cases.title: CIT v. Hindustan Coca Cola Beverages Pvt. Ltd.
cases.facts:
Hindustan Coca Cola paid warehousing charges to Pradeep Oil Corporation but failed to
deduct Tax Deducted at Source (TDS) under Section 194C (or deducted it at a lower rate). The
Income Tax Department classified Coca Cola as an 'assessee in default' under Section 201(1)
and demanded the recovery of the short-deducted TDS amount from Coca Cola. However , the
recipient (Pradeep Oil Corporation) had already declared this exact income in its own tax
returns and had fully paid the requisite income tax on it.
cases.issues:
1. Can the Revenue recover the TDS amount from the deductor (assessee in default) if
the deductee (recipient) has already paid the tax on that income?
2. Does double taxation apply to TDS defaults?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The assessee (Coca Cola) argued that TDS is merely a mechanism to collect the recipient's tax
in advance. If the recipient has already paid their final tax liability, forcing Coca Cola to pay
the TDS again amounts to illegal double recovery by the government.
B. Defendant / Revenue / State
The Revenue argued that the statutory liability to deduct TDS is independent. The default
crystallizes the moment the deduction is missed, making the deductor strictly liable
regardless of what the recipient does later .
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the assessee, holding that the TDS cannot be
recovered if the deductee has paid the tax.
cases.reasoning:
The Court brought pragmatism to the TDS recovery mechanism. It held that the purpose of
TDS is not to create an independent tax, but merely to facilitate the collection of the
deductee's income tax. If the primary tax liability is already discharged by the recipient (the
deductee), the government has suffered no loss of revenue. Permitting the government to
recover the TDS amount from the deductor after the deductee has paid the tax would amount
to unjust enrichment and double taxation. Therefore, while the deductor remains an 'assessee
in default' and is liable to pay interest (under Sec 201(1A)) for the delay and face penalties, the
actual principal amount of the TDS cannot be recovered from them.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. The principal TDS amount cannot be recovered from a deductor if the deductee has
already paid the tax on that income.
2. Double recovery of tax is prohibited in the TDS framework.
3. The deductor remains liable for interest and penalties for the period of the default.

cases.title: CIT v. Smifs Securities Ltd.
cases.facts:
Smifs Securities Ltd. underwent an amalgamation process. The company claimed
depreciation on the 'goodwill' that arose out of the amalgamation (calculated as the difference
between the cost of the assets acquired and the value of shares allotted). The Assessing Officer
disallowed the depreciation, arguing that 'goodwill' is not explicitly listed as an intangible
asset under Section 32(1)(ii) of the Income Tax Act.
cases.issues:
1. Does 'goodwill' fall under the definition of an intangible asset eligible for
depreciation under Section 32 of the ITA?
2. Is the principle of ejusdem generis applicable to the expression 'any other business or
commercial rights of similar nature'?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The Revenue argued that Section 32 specifically lists 'know-how, patents, copyrights,
trademarks, licences, franchises'. Since goodwill is not explicitly mentioned, it cannot be
deemed an eligible intangible asset.
B. Defendant / Revenue / State
The assessee argued that the phrase 'any other business or commercial rights of similar
nature' acts as a catch-all. Goodwill is a commercial right generated through business
combinations that brings future economic benefit.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the assessee, classifying goodwill as a
depreciable intangible asset.
cases.reasoning:
The Court read Section 32(1)(ii) expansively. Applying the principle of ejusdem generis, the
Court held that 'goodwill' generated during a corporate amalgamation constitutes a
commercial right of a similar nature to trademarks, patents, and licenses. Goodwill possesses
the essential characteristic of an intangible asset that diminishes in value or is amortized
over time in the books. Therefore, the difference between the consideration paid and the net
value of the assets taken over , representing goodwill, is a depreciable asset under the Income
Tax Act.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. 'Goodwill' is recognized as an intangible asset under Section 32(1)(ii) of the ITA.
2. Depreciation can be legally claimed on goodwill arising from amalgamation or
acquisition.
3. The statutory phrase 'any other business or commercial rights of similar nature'
includes goodwill.

cases.title: Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills v. State of UP
cases.facts:
The State Government of Uttar Pradesh made a categorical announcement offering a three-
year exemption from sales tax to all new industrial units established in the state to promote
industrialization. Relying on this explicit promise, the appellant company borrowed massive
funds and set up a new sugar factory. However , before the factory could commence
production, the State Government abruptly rescinded the exemption. The company
challenged this reversal.
cases.issues:
1. Does the doctrine of 'Promissory Estoppel' apply against the State in matters of
taxation and executive policy?
2. Can the State arbitrarily withdraw a tax exemption after a party has altered its
position based on the State's promise?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The company argued that it had altered its economic position solely based on the
government's categorical assurance. Withdrawing the exemption would cause ruinous
financial losses, invoking promissory estoppel.
B. Defendant / Revenue / State
The State argued that there can be no estoppel against the exercise of sovereign legislative or
executive powers. Tax exemptions are matters of public policy and can be withdrawn at any
time to protect state revenue.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the company, firmly applying the doctrine of
promissory estoppel against the Government.
cases.reasoning:
In a landmark administrative and tax law judgment, the Court held that the State is not
exempt from liability if it makes a promise knowing that the other party will act on it. If a
citizen alters their position to their detriment based on a government's promise of tax
exemption, the government is legally bound by that promise. The Court ruled that the
doctrine of promissory estoppel applies against the executive. The only exception is if the
State can prove that overriding public interest absolutely necessitates the withdrawal of the
promise, and even then, courts will scrutinize the claim strictly. Here, the State failed to show
such overriding public interest.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. The doctrine of Promissory Estoppel is fully applicable against the Government in tax
exemption matters.
2. The State cannot arbitrarily withdraw a promised tax exemption if the taxpayer has
altered their economic position based on it.
3. Sovereign immunity does not justify breaking executive promises unless
overwhelming public interest is proven.

cases.title: CIT v. Excel Industries Ltd.
cases.facts:
The assessee exported goods and became entitled to advance licenses (import duty
entitlements) under a government scheme. The Revenue sought to tax the value of these
entitlements in the year the exports were made. The assessee argued that the benefit should
be taxed only in the subsequent year when the imports were actually made and the duty
exemption was utilized. Furthermore, in previous assessment years, the Revenue had
accepted the assessee's method of taxing it in the subsequent year .
cases.issues:
1. At what point does the income from import entitlements 'accrue' for taxation
purposes?
2. Does the 'Principle of Consistency' prevent the Revenue from arbitrarily changing its
stance from one assessment year to another?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The Revenue argued that under the mercantile system, the right to receive the benefit
accrued the moment the exports were completed, triggering the tax liability immediately.
B. Defendant / Revenue / State
The assessee argued that real income had not accrued because the imports had not occurred.
They also heavily relied on the principle of consistency, pointing out the Revenue's past
acceptance of their accounting method.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the assessee based on the accrual of real income
and the principle of consistency.
cases.reasoning:
First, the Court held that income accrues when it becomes a reality. Earning an entitlement is
not enough; the benefit is strictly hypothetical until the assessee actually imports goods and
uses the license to offset duty. Secondly, and more crucially, the Court enforced the Principle
of Consistency. While the strict doctrine of res judicata does not apply to tax proceedings
(every assessment year is distinct), the Revenue cannot arbitrarily flip-flop its stance on the
exact same legal and factual matrix. If the tax authorities have accepted an accounting
method in previous years, they cannot suddenly reject it in a later year without any fresh
facts or changes in the law, as it causes severe harassment to taxpayers.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. The Principle of Consistency applies in tax laws; Revenue cannot arbitrarily change its
stance without material changes in facts or law.
2. While res judicata doesn't strictly apply, courts require certainty and finality in
repetitive tax assessments.
3. Hypothetical benefits (like unutilized import entitlements) do not constitute accrued
real income.

cases.title: CIT v. Ponni Sugars & Chemicals Ltd.
cases.facts:
To incentivize the setting up of new sugar factories and the expansion of existing ones, the
Government introduced a scheme providing subsidies to sugar manufacturers. The subsidy
was linked to the increased production of sugar . The Revenue sought to tax this subsidy as a
'revenue receipt' (taxable income) because it was calculated based on the day-to-day
production output. The assessee argued it was a 'capital receipt' (non-taxable) because the
overarching purpose of the scheme was to help them repay term loans taken for setting up
the new plant machinery.
cases.issues:
1. What is the test to determine whether a government subsidy is a taxable 'revenue
receipt' or a non-taxable 'capital receipt'?
2. Does the mode of calculation (linked to production) determine the nature of the
subsidy?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The Revenue argued that since the subsidy amount was quantified based on the amount of
sugar produced and sold, it was intimately connected to the day-to-day trading operations,
making it a revenue receipt.
B. Defendant / Revenue / State
The assessee argued that the objective of the grant was to fund capital expansion. The
calculation method is merely a mechanism, not the defining character of the grant.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the assessee, establishing the 'Purpose Test' for
classifying subsidies.
cases.reasoning:
The Court laid down the definitive 'Purpose Test'. The character of a subsidy (whether capital
or revenue) does not depend on its source, the form it takes, or the mathematical formula
used to calculate it. The sole criterion is the purpose for which the subsidy is given. If a
subsidy is given to assist the assessee in carrying out business operations more profitably or
to meet daily working capital requirements, it is a revenue receipt. However , if the object of
the subsidy is to enable the assessee to set up a new plant, expand capacity, or acquire capital
assets, it is a capital receipt. Because the scheme explicitly aimed to help sugar mills repay
capital term loans for machinery, it was a capital receipt, regardless of being quantified by
production output.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. The 'Purpose Test' determines the taxability of a government subsidy.
2. Subsidies given to acquire capital assets or set up a new business are non-taxable
capital receipts.
3. The mathematical formula or mechanism used to calculate the subsidy is irrelevant to
its legal character .

cases.title: G. Venkataswami Naidu & Co. v. CIT
cases.facts:
The assessee firm, acting as managing agents for a textile mill, purchased four contiguous
plots of land adjacent to the mill over several years. The firm never used the land for any
agricultural or personal purpose. Eventually, the firm sold all four plots to the textile mill at a
massive profit. The Revenue sought to tax this profit as business income, arguing the
transaction was an 'adventure in the nature of trade'. The assessee claimed it was a mere
capital investment resulting in capital gains.
cases.issues:
1. How does tax law distinguish between a mere 'capital investment' and an 'adventure
in the nature of trade'?
2. Does an isolated transaction of purchase and sale of land qualify as a business
activity?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The assessee argued that dealing in land was not their normal business. Buying property and
selling it years later at a profit is a classic capital investment strategy, not a trading venture.
B. Defendant / Revenue / State
The Revenue argued that the assessee deliberately purchased plots right next to the mill they
managed, knowing the mill would eventually need to expand. The sole intention was to
corner the land and extract a high price, which is a pure trading motive.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Revenue, holding the transaction was an
adventure in the nature of trade.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that even a single, isolated transaction can constitute an 'adventure in the
nature of trade'. There is no rigid mathematical formula; it depends on the totality of facts.
The critical test is the initial intention of the assessee at the time of purchase. If land is
bought with the sole and exclusive intention to resell it at a profit, and the purchaser takes
steps to increase its value or targets a specific buyer , it points to a trading motive. The Court
noted the assessee purchased land specifically adjacent to their principal's mill, knowing the
mill's expansion needs, and held onto it without any other use until the mill was forced to buy
it. This was a calculated commercial maneuver , making the profit taxable as business income.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. An isolated transaction can be taxed as business income if it qualifies as an 'adventure
in the nature of trade'.
2. The dominant initial intention at the time of purchase determines whether it is an
investment or a trade.
3. Buying property with the sole, targeted intention of reselling it at a profit to a specific
buyer indicates a trading motive.

cases.title: Navnit Lal C. Javeri v. K.K. Sen
cases.facts:
Navnit Lal, a major shareholder in a closely held private company, took substantial cash loans
from the company. The company had accumulated profits. Under Section 2(22)(e) of the
Income Tax Act (formerly Sec 2(6A)(e)), any advance or loan made by a company (in which
the public are not substantially interested) to a shareholder holding at least 10% voting power
is treated as 'deemed dividend' to the extent the company possesses accumulated profits. The
ITO taxed the loan as dividend income. The assessee challenged the constitutional validity of
this section.
cases.issues:
1. Can the legislature legally classify a repayable loan as 'income' (deemed dividend) for
taxation purposes?
2. Does Section 2(22)(e) violate the legislative competence under Entry 82, List I (Taxes
on income)?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The assessee argued that a loan is a liability, not income. By definition, income must be an
inflow of wealth. Taxing a debt as income is an artificial, unconstitutional legal fiction
exceeding Parliament's power to tax 'income'.
B. Defendant / Revenue / State
The Revenue argued the provision was introduced as an anti-evasion measure. Closely held
companies were masking dividend payouts as 'loans' to their controlling shareholders to
avoid dividend tax.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: A Constitution Bench upheld the constitutional validity of the 'deemed dividend'
provision under Section 2(22)(e).
cases.reasoning:
The Court applied the doctrine of 'ancillary and incidental powers'. While a loan is not
inherently income, Parliament has the power to enact anti-evasion provisions to prevent the
evasion of income tax. The Court noted that controlling shareholders in private companies
frequently extracted accumulated corporate profits disguised as 'loans' which were never
practically repaid, bypassing dividend distribution tax. Creating a legal fiction to deem such
loans as dividends is a valid exercise of legislative power designed to plug massive revenue
leakage. The fiction is strictly limited to closely held companies and specific controlling
shareholders, making it a reasonable and constitutional classification.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Parliament has the constitutional competence to create legal fictions to tax capital
receipts (like loans) as 'income' to prevent tax evasion.
2. Section 2(22)(e) taxing loans as 'deemed dividends' is a valid anti-evasion measure.
3. The doctrine of ancillary powers allows the legislature to enact strict rules to plug
revenue leakage in closely held companies.

cases.title: Ishikawajima-Harima Heavy Industries Ltd. v. DIT
cases.facts:
A Japanese consortium (the assessee) entered into a massive turnkey contract with Petronet
LNG in India to set up an LNG receiving terminal. The contract involved offshore supply of
equipment, offshore services (design in Japan), onshore supply, and onshore services
(construction in India). The contract explicitly stated that the title and ownership of the
offshore equipment transferred to the Indian buyer on the high seas (outside Indian
territory). The Revenue sought to tax the entire contract value, including the offshore supply
and services, in India.
cases.issues:
1. Is the income from the offshore supply of goods and offshore services taxable in India
under Section 9(1) of the ITA if the contract is a composite turnkey project?
2. What constitutes a sufficient territorial nexus to tax offshore transactions?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The Revenue argued that it was an indivisible, composite turnkey contract. Since the ultimate
project was erected and utilized in India, the entire profit accrued in India, establishing a
complete territorial nexus.
B. Defendant / Revenue / State
The assessee argued that the contract prices were clearly apportioned. The offshore
equipment sale was completed outside India (title passed on the high seas). Therefore, the
profits from the offshore elements did not accrue in India.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the assessee, holding that offshore supplies and
offshore services in a divisible contract are not taxable in India.
cases.reasoning:
The Court established the principle of territoriality in composite contracts. It held that even in
a turnkey project, if the contract clearly apportions consideration for offshore and onshore
activities, they must be treated separately. For the offshore supply of goods, the Court found
that the property/title passed to the Indian buyer outside India, and the payment was
received outside India. Therefore, the sale concluded outside the territory, and no income
accrued in India. For the offshore services (design), the Court held that for Section 9(1)(vii) to
apply, the services must be both rendered in India and utilized in India. Since the design was
rendered entirely in Japan, it fell outside the Indian tax net.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. In divisible turnkey contracts, offshore supply of goods where title passes outside
India is not taxable in India.
2. To tax 'Fees for Technical Services' (prior to legislative amendments), the services had
to be rendered and utilized in India.
3. The concept of a territorial nexus cannot be stretched to tax transactions completed
entirely outside the sovereign territory.

cases.title: CIT v. T.V. Sundaram Iyengar & Sons Ltd.
cases.facts:
The assessee company received trade deposits/advances from its customers during the course
of business. Over several years, some of these deposits were never claimed by the customers.
The statutory limitation period for recovering these debts expired. The assessee transferred
these unclaimed trade balances from its liability account and credited them to its Profit &
Loss (P&L) account as a surplus. The ITO taxed this amount as business income under Section
41(1) of the ITA.
cases.issues:
1. Do unclaimed trade advances, which were originally capital receipts, become taxable
revenue income when written back to the P&L account?
2. Does Section 41(1) (cessation of trading liability) apply to such unclaimed deposits?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The assessee argued that the deposits were received as security/capital receipts, not as trading
income. A capital receipt does not magically transform into a revenue receipt just by the
passage of time or a book entry.
B. Defendant / Revenue / State
The Revenue argued that the money was received in the course of trading operations. Once
the liability to repay extinguished and the company took the money to its P&L account as its
own profit, it became taxable business income.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Revenue, holding the written-back amounts
as taxable business income.
cases.reasoning:
The Court formulated a pragmatic principle. While the deposits were indeed capital receipts
when originally taken, their character changed over time. The money was received during
ordinary trading transactions. When the claims became time-barred, the assessee's liability to
repay extinguished. By transferring the amount to the P&L account, the assessee treated the
money as its own free operational surplus. The Court held that if an amount is received in the
course of a trading transaction, and ultimately becomes the absolute property of the assessee
due to the cessation of the liability to repay, it partakes the character of a taxable revenue
receipt. Book entries reflecting this reality trigger the tax.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Unclaimed trade deposits/advances transform into taxable revenue income when the
liability to repay ceases and the amount is appropriated by the assessee.
2. A capital receipt can metamorphose into a revenue receipt based on subsequent
events and accounting treatment.
3. Writing back unclaimed liabilities to the P&L account triggers taxation under the
principles of Section 41(1).

cases.title: Sahara India (Firm) v. CIT
cases.facts:
During the assessment proceedings of Sahara India, the Assessing Officer (AO), suspecting
massive complexities in the accounts, passed an order under Section 142(2A) of the ITA
directing the assessee to subject its accounts to a 'Special Audit' by a chartered accountant
nominated by the Revenue. A special audit imposes severe financial burdens on the assessee
(who has to pay the auditor) and delays assessments. The AO issued this directive without
giving Sahara India a prior hearing.
cases.issues:
1. Does an Assessing Officer have to follow the principles of natural justice and give a
pre-decisional hearing before ordering a Special Audit under Section 142(2A)?
2. Are administrative orders causing civil consequences subject to audi alteram
partem?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The assessee argued that a Special Audit causes immense prejudice, financial loss, and
reputational damage. It is an adverse civil consequence requiring a mandatory opportunity to
be heard before the order is passed.
B. Defendant / Revenue / State
The Revenue argued that ordering an audit is merely a step in the investigation/assessment
process, not a final penalty. Therefore, natural justice does not apply at this intermediate
procedural stage.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the assessee, mandating a pre-decisional hearing
for Special Audits.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that the phrase 'civil consequences' covers everything that affects a citizen in
their civil life, including financial and reputational impacts. A Special Audit under Section
142(2A) is not a routine step; it casts a heavy financial burden on the taxpayer and extends
the limitation period for assessment. Because it entails adverse civil consequences, the
requirement of audi alteram partem (right to be heard) is implicitly built into the provision,
even if the statute is silent. The AO must issue a show-cause notice, share the reasons why the
accounts are deemed excessively complex, and hear the assessee's objections before directing
the special audit.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Directing a Special Audit under Section 142(2A) entails adverse civil consequences for
the taxpayer .
2. The principles of natural justice require the Assessing Officer to grant a pre-decisional
hearing before ordering a special audit.
3. Tax authorities cannot use special audits routinely or arbitrarily without objective
justification.

cases.title: Southern Technologies Ltd. v. Joint CIT
cases.facts:
The assessee, an NBFC (Non-Banking Financial Company), was mandated by the Reserve Bank
of India (RBI) Prudential Norms to make a provision in its balance sheet for Non-Performing
Assets (NPAs). The NBFC created this provision and sought a tax deduction for it under
Section 36(1)(vii) of the ITA (bad debts). The Revenue disallowed the deduction, pointing out
that an RBI-mandated 'provision' for doubtful debts is not the same as an actual 'write-off' of
a bad debt required by the Income Tax Act.
cases.issues:
1. Do the RBI Prudential Norms override the specific provisions of the Income Tax Act
regarding deductions for bad debts?
2. Is a mere 'provision' for an NPA deductible under Section 36(1)(vii)?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The assessee argued that they were legally bound by RBI directives to classify these assets as
NPAs and provision for them. Tax law should align with the mandatory accounting
regulations imposed by the central banking regulator .
B. Defendant / Revenue / State
The Revenue argued that RBI guidelines are for capital adequacy and depositor protection,
whereas the ITA is strictly for computing taxable income. The ITA demands an actual write-
off, not a mere provision.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Revenue, holding that RBI guidelines do not
override the Income Tax Act.
cases.reasoning:
The Court drew a sharp distinction between regulatory accounting and tax accounting. The
RBI Prudential Norms are designed to reflect the true financial health of an NBFC to protect
depositors. However , the Income Tax Act is a self-contained code for determining taxable
income. Section 36(1)(vii) explicitly requires a bad debt to be actually 'written off' as
irrecoverable in the accounts. A mere 'provision' for doubtful debts anticipates a future loss;
it is not an actual write-off of the asset. The Court categorically held that RBI directions cannot
override the mandatory statutory requirements of the ITA. Therefore, the provision for NPAs
was added back to the taxable income.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. RBI Prudential Norms and accounting guidelines do not override the strict statutory
provisions of the Income Tax Act.
2. A mere 'provision' for doubtful debts (NPAs) is not deductible as a bad debt under
Section 36(1)(vii).
3. Tax law requires an actual write-off of the debt to claim a deduction.

cases.title: K.C. Builders v. Assistant CIT
cases.facts:
The Income Tax Department levied a heavy penalty on K.C. Builders for 'concealment of
income' under Section 271(1)(c) of the ITA. Simultaneously, based on the same facts, the
Department launched criminal prosecution against the partners under Section 276C for
willful evasion of tax. The assessee challenged the civil penalty before the Income Tax
Appellate Tribunal (ITAT). The ITAT struck down the penalty, finding there was no
concealment. The assessee then approached the High Court to quash the criminal
prosecution, arguing it could not survive without the underlying penalty. The High Court
refused.
cases.issues:
1. Can criminal prosecution for tax evasion under Section 276C proceed if the
foundational civil penalty for concealment has been struck down by the ITAT?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The assessee argued that the criminal charge and the civil penalty were based on the exact
same set of facts and findings. If the highest fact-finding tribunal (ITAT) exonerates them of
concealment, the criminal prosecution is groundless and an abuse of process.
B. Defendant / Revenue / State
The Revenue argued that civil penalty proceedings and criminal prosecutions are distinct,
parallel procedures with different standards of proof, and one does not automatically
terminate the other .
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the assessee, quashing the criminal prosecution.
cases.reasoning:
The Court established a crucial protection for taxpayers against dual harassment. It held that
while penalty and prosecution are independent proceedings in theory, they are inextricably
linked when based on the identical factual matrix of 'concealment'. The ITAT is the ultimate
fact-finding authority under the ITA. If the ITAT categorically concludes that there was no
concealment of income and drops the penalty, the very foundation of the criminal charge
under Section 276C evaporates. Allowing a criminal trial to continue when the underlying
civil tax offense has been disproved on merits would be a mockery of justice and a futile
exercise. The criminal proceedings were therefore quashed.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Criminal prosecution for tax evasion under Section 276C cannot survive if the civil
penalty for concealment is cancelled by the ITAT on merits.
2. Exoneration by the final fact-finding authority in penalty proceedings removes the
foundation for criminal charges on the same facts.
3. Courts will quash such criminal proceedings to prevent the abuse of the legal process.

cases.title: CIT v. Rajendra Prasad Moody
cases.facts:
The assessee borrowed money from a bank and used it exclusively to purchase shares in
certain companies. He paid interest on this borrowed capital. During the relevant assessment
year , those companies did not declare any dividends, so he received zero income from those
shares. He claimed a deduction for the interest paid under Section 57(iii) of the ITA
(expenditure laid out wholly for making/earning income from other sources). The ITO
disallowed the deduction because no actual income (dividend) was earned that year to offset
the expense.
cases.issues:
1. Can a taxpayer claim a deduction for expenditure incurred to earn 'Income from
Other Sources' under Section 57(iii) if no actual income is received in that specific
assessment year?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The Revenue argued a strict matching principle: deductions can only be allowed against
income actually earned. If the income is zero, there is nothing from which to deduct the
expenditure.
B. Defendant / Revenue / State
The assessee argued that the statute requires the expenditure to be incurred 'for the purpose
of making or earning income'. It does not mandate that the effort must successfully result in
actual income in the same year .
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the assessee, allowing the deduction for interest
even without actual dividend income.
cases.reasoning:
The Court applied a purposive interpretation to Section 57(iii). It noted that the language of
the statute says 'expenditure laid out or expended wholly and exclusively for the purpose of
making or earning such income'. The phrase emphasizes the purpose of the expenditure,
not its result. A businessman borrows money and buys shares intending to earn dividends.
Whether the company ultimately declares a dividend is beyond his control. The legal
character of the expenditure as a deductible expense is established at the moment it is
incurred for an income-earning objective. Thus, the interest paid is fully deductible even if
the dividend yield in that particular year is absolute zero.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Deduction under Section 57(iii) depends on the purpose of the expenditure, not the
successful generation of actual income.
2. Interest paid on capital borrowed to buy shares is deductible even if no dividend is
declared in that assessment year .
3. The law evaluates the intent behind the investment, not its immediate fruition.

cases.title: Queen's Educational Society v. CIT
cases.facts:
An educational society ran schools and claimed tax exemption under Section 10(23C)(iiiad) of
the ITA, which exempts institutions existing 'solely for educational purposes and not for
purposes of profit'. The Income Tax Department observed that the society had consistently
generated a significant financial surplus (profit) over several years. Believing this proved a
profit-making motive, the Revenue stripped the society of its tax-exempt status. Several High
Courts had conflicting views on whether generating a surplus disqualified an educational
institution.
cases.issues:
1. Does generating a financial surplus automatically destroy the 'charitable' and 'non-
profit' status of an educational institution under Section 10(23C)?
2. What is the correct test to determine if an institution exists 'solely for educational
purposes'?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The Revenue argued that the words 'not for purposes of profit' must be strictly construed. A
consistent generation of massive surpluses proves the institution is running as a commercial
business, not a charity.
B. Defendant / Revenue / State
The assessee argued that generating a surplus is necessary for the survival and expansion of
the school. The crucial test is not the generation of surplus, but what the surplus is used for
(ploughed back into education).
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the educational societies, holding that
generating a surplus does not strip them of tax exemption.
cases.reasoning:
The Court settled the law by adopting a holistic test. The mere generation of a surplus at the
end of the year does not mean the institution exists for the 'purpose of profit'. To maintain
infrastructure, build new classrooms, and upgrade facilities, an educational institution must
generate some surplus. The definitive test is the application of that surplus. If the profit is
ploughed back entirely into the educational institution for its development and is not
siphoned off for the personal benefit of the founders, trustees, or management, the institution
retains its charitable character . An institution is only stripped of its exemption if education is
merely a cloak to hide a commercial profit-making machine for personal wealth
accumulation.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Generating a financial surplus does not inherently disqualify an educational
institution from tax exemption under Sec 10(23C).
2. The critical test is whether the surplus is ploughed back into education or siphoned off
for personal gain.
3. 'Not for purposes of profit' means the ultimate objective must be education, not
enriching the founders.

cases.title: State of UP v. Renusagar Power Co.
cases.facts:
Hindustan Aluminium Corp. (Hindalco) set up a wholly-owned subsidiary, Renusagar Power
Co., to generate electricity exclusively for Hindalco's massive aluminum manufacturing plant.
Under the UP Electricity Duty Act, a lower rate of duty applied to electricity generated from a
company's 'own source' (captive generation), while a higher rate applied to electricity
purchased from outside. The State levied the higher duty on Hindalco, arguing that
Renusagar was a distinct corporate entity, meaning Hindalco was 'purchasing' power from an
outside source.
cases.issues:
1. Can the corporate veil be lifted in taxation matters to treat a holding company and its
100% captive subsidiary as a single economic entity?
2. Does Renusagar's power generation qualify as Hindalco's 'own source' of electricity?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The State relied on the strict doctrine of corporate personality (Salomon v. Salomon), arguing
that Renusagar and Hindalco are distinct legal persons. Therefore, the power transfer is a
commercial sale attracting higher duty.
B. Defendant / Revenue / State
The assessee argued that Renusagar was created merely as an administrative necessity. It sold
100% of its power to Hindalco, had the same directors, and Hindalco exercised total control.
Piercing the veil would show it is captive generation.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court pierced the corporate veil, treating Hindalco and Renusagar as a
single entity, thereby allowing the lower duty rate.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that the concept of lifting the corporate veil is constantly expanding in
economic and tax law. When a subsidiary is completely dominated and controlled by the
holding company to the extent that it has no independent existence, and is created solely to
facilitate the holding company's core business, the courts will ignore the separate legal
facade. The Court found that Renusagar generated power exclusively for Hindalco, made no
independent profit, and was totally financially and administratively integrated with Hindalco.
Recognizing the economic reality over legal technicality, the Court ruled that the power plant
was effectively Hindalco's 'own source' of generation, entitling them to the lower rate of
electricity duty.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. The corporate veil can be lifted in tax and regulatory matters to ascertain the true
economic reality of an enterprise.
2. A 100% captive subsidiary with no independent operations can be treated as a single
entity with the holding company.
3. Taxation must consider the substance of the transaction over its strict corporate form.

cases.title: CIT v. Saurashtra Cement & Chemical Industries Ltd.
cases.facts:
The assessee company entered into an agreement with a supplier to purchase plant and
machinery to set up a cement manufacturing unit. The contract contained a liquidated
damages clause: if the supplier delayed the delivery of the machinery, they would have to pay
a penalty. The supplier defaulted, and the assessee received a substantial amount as
liquidated damages. The Revenue sought to tax this amount as a 'revenue receipt' (business
income), arguing it compensated for the loss of business profits due to the delay.
cases.issues:
1. Are liquidated damages received for a delay in the supply of capital assets
(machinery) considered a taxable 'revenue receipt' or a non-taxable 'capital receipt'?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The Revenue argued that because the delay in setting up the machinery delayed production,
the damages essentially compensated the company for the hypothetical loss of operational
profits. Compensation for loss of profit is a revenue receipt.
B. Defendant / Revenue / State
The assessee argued that the machinery was the fixed capital framework of the company. The
damages related directly to the acquisition of a capital asset, making it a capital receipt.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the assessee, classifying the liquidated damages
as a non-taxable capital receipt.
cases.reasoning:
The Court focused on the source and purpose of the damages. The compensation was
intimately linked to the acquisition of the plant and machinery, which is the capital apparatus
or profit-making apparatus of the business. The damages were not for a breach of a regular
trading or commercial contract (which would yield revenue), but for a breach of a contract to
build the fixed capital structure of the company. The Court held that compensation linked to
the impairment, delay, or sterilization of the capital structure is inherently a capital receipt. It
reduces the overall capital cost of the project and does not constitute taxable business
income.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Liquidated damages received for a delay in the supply of plant/machinery are capital
receipts.
2. Compensation related to the fixed capital apparatus of a business is not taxable as
revenue income.
3. The character of the receipt is determined by the nature of the asset (capital vs. stock-
in-trade) it replaces or compensates for .

cases.title: Canon India Pvt. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Customs
cases.facts:
Officers of the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence (DRI) initiated an investigation against
Canon India and issued a Show Cause Notice (SCN) demanding recovery of customs duty
under Section 28(4) of the Customs Act. Section 28 states that 'the proper officer' shall issue
the notice. Canon challenged the SCN, arguing that DRI officers are not the 'proper officers'
under the Customs Act to reopen an assessment that was originally cleared by the regular
Customs Officers at the port.
cases.issues:
1. Do officers of the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence (DRI) have the jurisdiction to
issue Show Cause Notices for recovery of duty under Section 28 of the Customs Act?
2. What is the strict definition of 'the proper officer'?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
Canon argued that 'the proper officer' means the specific officer who originally assessed the
goods, or their direct successor . Allowing an external intelligence agency (DRI) to reopen
assessments bypasses statutory jurisdiction.
B. Defendant / Revenue / State
The Revenue argued that the Government had issued notifications appointing DRI officers as
Customs Officers, granting them concurrent jurisdiction to protect the revenue from fraud
across the country.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court quashed the SCN, ruling that DRI officers do not have the
jurisdiction to issue recovery notices under Section 28.
cases.reasoning:
The Court applied a strict literal interpretation to the Customs Act. It noted that the statute
specifically uses the article 'the' proper officer , not 'a' proper officer . This denotes the specific
officer who was assigned the original duty of assessment. Parliament intended to prevent
administrative chaos where multiple agencies could arbitrarily reopen cleared goods. The
Court held that unless a DRI officer has been specifically designated under Section 2(34) of the
Act to perform the functions of assessment, they cannot issue an SCN. General notifications
making them 'customs officers' do not automatically give them the adjudicatory power of 'the
proper officer'. This judgment invalidated thousands of pending DRI notices.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Strict interpretation of statutory jurisdiction: 'the proper officer' means the specific
assessing officer , not just any customs officer .
2. DRI officers lack the inherent jurisdiction to issue SCNs for duty recovery under
Section 28 of the Customs Act.
3. Jurisdictional defects in issuing a show-cause notice render the entire subsequent tax
proceedings void.

cases.title: Commissioner of Central Excise v. Fiat India Pvt. Ltd.
cases.facts:
Fiat India sold its cars (Fiat Uno) at a price significantly below their actual cost of production
for a sustained period. They did this strategically to penetrate the highly competitive Indian
market. They paid Central Excise duty based on this lowered, actual selling price. The
Revenue challenged this valuation, arguing that the selling price was not the 'sole
consideration' for the sale. The Revenue rejected the invoice value and assessed the duty
based on the actual cost of production plus a nominal profit margin.
cases.issues:
1. Can the Revenue reject the actual transaction value for excise duty if a manufacturer
deliberately sells goods below the cost of production for market penetration?
2. Does market penetration constitute an 'extra-commercial consideration'?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The Revenue argued that no prudent businessman sells below cost for years. The massive
losses were borne to build a market base, meaning the true 'consideration' included the
invisible benefit of market penetration, justifying the rejection of the invoice price.
B. Defendant / Revenue / State
The assessee argued that Section 4 of the Central Excise Act states duty must be paid on the
actual transaction value. Unless the Revenue proves there was an under-the-table flow of
extra cash, the invoice price cannot be discarded just because the business is making a loss.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Revenue, allowing them to reject the
transaction value and assess duty based on the cost of production.
cases.reasoning:
This is a highly controversial ruling regarding valuation. The Court held that under Section 4
of the Excise Act, the transaction value is acceptable only if the price is the 'sole consideration'
for the sale. The Court reasoned that Fiat's deliberate strategy to sell below cost for an
extended period was an 'extra-commercial consideration' (market penetration). The price
charged did not reflect the true value of the goods; it was artificially suppressed to gain a
foothold. Because the price was tainted by this extra-commercial strategy, it ceased to be the
'sole consideration'. Therefore, the Revenue was justified in invoking the Valuation Rules to
determine the true value based on manufacturing costs. (Note: This judgment caused
massive unrest in industries adopting predatory pricing strategies)..
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Selling goods deliberately below the cost of production for 'market penetration'
constitutes an extra-commercial consideration.
2. If the invoice price is not the 'sole consideration', the Revenue can reject the
transaction value for excise assessment.
3. Predatory pricing strategies expose manufacturers to tax liabilities based on actual
production costs.

cases.title: State of Karnataka v. Ecom Gill Coffee Trading Private Limited
cases.facts:
Under the Karnataka Value Added Tax (KVAT) Act (principles directly applicable to GST),
dealers claimed Input Tax Credit (ITC) based on tax invoices issued by their suppliers. The
suppliers had collected the tax from Ecom Gill but allegedly failed to deposit it with the
government. The tax authorities denied the ITC to Ecom Gill, demanding they prove the actual
physical movement of goods. Ecom Gill argued that producing valid tax invoices and bank
statements proving payment to the supplier was sufficient to claim ITC.
cases.issues:
1. What is the burden of proof on a purchasing dealer to claim Input Tax Credit?
2. Is the mere production of tax invoices and bank payment proofs sufficient to claim
ITC if the physical delivery of goods is questioned?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The purchasing dealer argued they are bona fide buyers. Once they produce a valid invoice
and prove payment through banking channels, they have discharged their statutory duty.
They cannot be penalized if the supplier defaults or vanishes.
B. Defendant / Revenue / State
The Revenue argued that ITC is a concession, and strict proof is required. Invoices can be fake
(bill trading). The dealer must conclusively prove the actual physical receipt and movement
of the goods to claim the credit.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Revenue, holding that invoices and payment
proofs are insufficient; actual physical movement of goods must be proven.
cases.reasoning:
The Court laid down a strict standard for claiming ITC, severely cracking down on circular
trading and fake invoicing. The Court held that the burden of proving entitlement to ITC lies
squarely on the purchasing dealer . Simply producing a tax invoice, an e-way bill, or a bank
account statement showing payment is not enough to discharge this burden. The dealer must
furnish concrete evidence of the actual physical movement and delivery of the goods-such
as lorry receipts, toll receipts, weighbridge slips, and the vehicle driver's details. If the dealer
fails to prove that the goods actually physically moved from the supplier to them, the claim
for ITC must be denied, regardless of the financial transactions.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. The burden of proof to claim Input Tax Credit (ITC) lies absolutely on the purchasing
dealer .
2. Mere production of invoices and bank payment records is insufficient to claim ITC.
3. The dealer must conclusively prove the actual physical movement and receipt of goods
using transport documents.

cases.title: Radha Krishan Industries v. State of Himachal Pradesh
cases.facts:
The GST authorities, suspecting tax evasion through fraudulent input tax credits, invoked
Section 83 of the Himachal Pradesh Goods and Services Tax Act (HPGST) to 'provisionally
attach' the bank accounts and receivables of Radha Krishan Industries. This crippled the
company's daily business operations. The company challenged this action, arguing that the
power was being used routinely and arbitrarily without any pending formal proceedings
against them that necessitated such a draconian step.
cases.issues:
1. What are the limits on the power of tax authorities to provisionally attach a
taxpayer's bank accounts under Section 83 of the GST Act?
2. What safeguards must be followed before exercising this draconian power?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The taxpayer argued that attaching working capital paralyzes a running business. The power
under Section 83 should only be used as a last resort in extreme cases of flight risk, not as a
routine investigative tool.
B. Defendant / Revenue / State
The Revenue argued that protecting government revenue is paramount. Given the massive
scale of GST fraud, provisional attachment is a necessary statutory tool to prevent the
taxpayer from siphoning off funds before the assessment is complete.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the taxpayer , establishing strict guidelines to
curb the arbitrary use of provisional attachment powers.
cases.reasoning:
The Court described the power of provisional attachment under Section 83 as a draconian
and harsh power that fundamentally impacts the fundamental right to carry on a business
under Article 19(1)(g). The Court held that this power must be exercised only in exceptional
circumstances where there is substantial, concrete evidence that the taxpayer is about to
dispose of assets to thwart the recovery of tax. The Commissioner must form a 'formal
opinion' based on tangible material that attachment is 'necessary to protect the interest of the
government revenue'. It cannot be based on mere suspicion, whims, or routine investigations.
Furthermore, attaching a running bank account should be the absolute last resort, as it causes
'civil death' to a business.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Provisional attachment of bank accounts under Section 83 of the GST Act is a
draconian power to be used strictly as a last resort.
2. The Commissioner must form a written, objective opinion based on tangible evidence
that the revenue is at immediate risk.
3. Routine attachment of working capital violates Article 19(1)(g) and paralyzes
legitimate businesses.

cases.title: CIT v. P.V.A.L. Kulandagan Chettiar
cases.facts:
The assessee, an Indian resident, owned rubber estates in Malaysia and earned capital gains
from the sale of these properties in Malaysia. He did not bring this income into India. The
Indian Income Tax Department sought to tax these capital gains, arguing that as a resident of
India, his global income is taxable under Section 5 of the ITA. The assessee invoked the India-
Malaysia Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement (DTAA), which stated that capital gains from
immovable property 'may be taxed' in the country where the property is situated.
cases.issues:
1. If a DTAA states that income 'may be taxed' in the foreign country, does it
automatically oust the taxation rights of the home country (India)?
2. Do DTAA provisions override the global income taxation principle of Section 5 of the
ITA?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The Revenue argued that the phrase 'may be taxed' in Malaysia means Malaysia has a right to
tax it, but it does not expressly prohibit India from taxing it as well. They offered to give
foreign tax credit for taxes paid in Malaysia.
B. Defendant / Revenue / State
The assessee argued that the purpose of a DTAA is to avoid double taxation entirely. By
allocating the taxing right to Malaysia (where the property is located), the treaty implicitly
strips India of its right to tax that specific income.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the assessee, holding that the DTAA overrides
the Income Tax Act and India has no right to tax the income.
cases.reasoning:
The Court reinforced the supremacy of tax treaties. Section 90(2) of the ITA dictates that DTAA
provisions prevail if they are more beneficial to the assessee. The Court interpreted the
phrase 'may be taxed' contextually. It held that when a DTAA explicitly allocates the right to
tax a specific category of income (like immovable property) to the country of source
(Malaysia), it inherently implies that the country of residence (India) surrenders its right to
tax that income. If both countries retained the right, it would lead to double taxation,
defeating the treaty's core purpose. Therefore, despite Section 5 taxing global income, the
treaty overrides it, and the Malaysian capital gains are completely exempt from Indian tax.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Double Taxation Avoidance Agreements (DTAAs) override the domestic Income Tax Act
if they are more beneficial (Section 90(2)).
2. The allocation of taxing rights to the source country in a DTAA implicitly ousts the
jurisdiction of the residence country to tax that income.
3. A resident's global income can be restricted from Indian taxation by explicit treaty
rules.

cases.title: G.E. India Technology Centre Pvt Ltd v. CIT
cases.facts:
G.E. India Technology Centre purchased off-the-shelf software from a foreign non-resident supplier. The Indian
Income Tax Department demanded that the company should have deducted Tax Deducted at Source (TDS)
under Section 195 of the Income Tax Act (ITA) before making the remittance abroad. The Department argued
that Section 195 imposes an absolute obligation to deduct tax on 'any sum' remitted to a non-resident,
regardless of whether the sum is ultimately taxable in India.
cases.issues:
1. Is the obligation to deduct TDS under Section 195 absolute for all remittances to non-residents?
2. Does Section 195 apply if the remitted sum is not chargeable to tax under the ITA?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The assessee argued that the software purchase payment was not 'royalty' but business income, which was not
taxable in India as the foreign supplier had no Permanent Establishment. If the income is not chargeable to tax
in India, the TDS mechanism under Section 195 cannot be triggered.
B. Defendant / Revenue
The Revenue argued a literal interpretation of Section 195, claiming that the payer must deduct tax on all
foreign remittances. If the payee believes the income is non-taxable, they must apply for a refund or a lower
withholding certificate under Section 195(2).
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the assessee, holding that TDS under Section 195 is only required
if the remitted sum is chargeable to tax in India.
cases.reasoning:
The Court clarified that the expression 'any other sum chargeable under the provisions of this Act' in Section
195 is critical. The withholding tax obligation is intrinsically linked to the chargeability of the income. If a
remittance does not contain any element of income that is taxable in India under the ITA or the relevant DTAA,
there is no statutory obligation to deduct TDS. The Revenue's argument that tax must be deducted blindly on
gross remittances, forcing non-residents to claim refunds, was rejected as it would cause immense hardship and
disrupt international trade. The obligation under Section 195 arises only if the payment is legally liable to
Indian income tax.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Section 195 TDS applies only if the sum remitted to a non-resident is chargeable to tax in India.
2. There is no absolute obligation to deduct tax on gross cross-border remittances.
3. The payer can independently determine if the payment is taxable before deducting TDS.

cases.title: I.C.D.S. Ltd. v. CIT
cases.facts:
I.C.D.S. Ltd. was a non-banking finance company engaged in the business of leasing vehicles. The company
purchased trucks and leased them to various transport operators. The vehicles were registered in the names of
the lessees (the transport operators) under the Motor Vehicles Act for operational convenience. I.C.D.S.
claimed depreciation on these trucks under Section 32 of the ITA. The Assessing Officer denied the
depreciation, arguing that the assessee was not the legal 'owner' (as the RC book showed the lessees' names)
and was not 'using' the vehicles for its own business.
cases.issues:
1. Can a leasing company claim depreciation on assets leased out to others?
2. Does registration under the Motor Vehicles Act exclusively determine 'ownership' for the purpose of
Section 32 depreciation?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The assessee argued that it financed and purchased the vehicles. Leasing them out was its core business.
Thus, it 'used' the assets for its leasing business and retained beneficial ownership, despite the RC book
registration.
B. Defendant / Revenue
The Revenue argued that Section 32 requires the assessee to both 'own' and 'use' the asset. Since the lessees
possessed the trucks, used them for transport, and held the RC books, the leasing company fulfilled neither
condition.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the assessee, allowing the depreciation claim on the leased
vehicles.
cases.reasoning:
The Court adopted a purposive interpretation of Section 32. Regarding 'ownership', the Court held that the
Motor Vehicles Act registration is not the ultimate test of ownership for income tax purposes. Since I.C.D.S.
paid for the trucks and had the right to repossess them upon lease default, it retained the real ownership.
Regarding 'use', the Court held that the phrase 'used for the purposes of the business' does not mean the
assessee must physically operate the asset. Since the assessee's business was leasing, leasing out the trucks
constituted the 'use' of the asset for its business. Therefore, both conditions of Section 32 were met.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. A leasing company 'uses' an asset for its business by leasing it out and can claim depreciation.
2. Registration under the Motor Vehicles Act is not conclusive proof of ownership for Section 32
depreciation.
3. Economic and beneficial ownership satisfies the 'ownership' requirement under the ITA.

cases.title: CIT v. Walfort Share and Stock Brokers P. Ltd.
cases.facts:
The assessee purchased mutual fund units just before the 'record date' for a dividend payout. After receiving the
massive tax-free dividend, the Net Asset Value (NA V) of the units naturally dropped. The assessee then sold the
units at this lower NA V , booking a short-term capital loss. The assessee used this capital loss to offset other
taxable income. This strategy is known as 'dividend stripping'. The Revenue disallowed the loss, invoking
Section 14A of the ITA, arguing that the loss was an 'expenditure incurred in relation to earning exempt
income' (the tax-free dividend).
cases.issues:
1. Is 'dividend stripping' a valid tax planning strategy or illegal tax evasion?
2. Does a capital loss booked due to a drop in NA V constitute an 'expenditure incurred' under Section
14A?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The Revenue argued that the entire transaction was a pre-planned, artificial device to create a fake loss and
evade taxes, violating the McDowell principle. Furthermore, the loss was intimately connected to earning the
exempt dividend, triggering Section 14A.
B. Defendant / Revenue
The assessee argued that buying and selling mutual funds is a legitimate market activity. A loss on the sale of
an asset is a 'loss', not an 'expenditure', and therefore Section 14A does not apply.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the assessee, allowing the capital loss and restricting the scope of
Section 14A.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that prior to the specific legislative insertion of Section 94(7) (which explicitly curbed dividend
stripping), the transaction was perfectly legal tax planning. The purchase and sale of units at market NA V were
genuine transactions, not sham devices. Crucially, the Court interpreted Section 14A, establishing a distinction
between a 'loss' and an 'expenditure'. Section 14A disallows deductions for 'expenditure incurred' to earn
exempt income (e.g., interest paid on loans taken to buy tax-free bonds). A capital loss arising from the sale of
an asset due to a drop in market value is not an 'expenditure incurred'. Therefore, Section 14A cannot be
invoked to disallow a capital loss.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. A capital loss on the sale of an asset is not an 'expenditure incurred' under Section 14A.
2. Genuine dividend stripping was a valid tax planning mechanism before the insertion of Section 94(7).
3. Section 14A applies only to actual outgoings/expenses specifically linked to earning exempt income.

cases.title: Formula One World Championship Ltd. v. CIT
cases.facts:
Formula One World Championship Ltd (FOWC), a UK company, entered into an agreement with Jaypee Sports
