to host the F1 Grand Prix in India at the Buddh International Circuit. FOWC granted Jaypee the right to host
the event but retained absolute control over the circuit, paddock, broadcasting rights, and commercial
exploitation during the event. The Revenue sought to tax FOWC's income in India, arguing that the Buddh
Circuit constituted a 'Fixed Place Permanent Establishment' (PE) for FOWC in India under the India-UK
DTAA.
cases.issues:
1. Does temporary but absolute control over a physical location (a race track) for a specific event
constitute a 'Fixed Place Permanent Establishment' (PE) under a DTAA?
2. Are the revenues earned by a non-resident from such an event taxable in India?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
FOWC argued that it did not own the track; it was only in India for three days a year for the race. A three-day
presence lacks the 'permanence' required to constitute a fixed place PE.
B. Defendant / Revenue
The Revenue argued that PE does not require ownership or 365-day presence. FOWC had complete physical
and commercial control over the track before and during the race, and its entire business model was predicated
on moving from circuit to circuit.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Revenue, holding that the Buddh International Circuit
constituted a Permanent Establishment for FOWC in India.
cases.reasoning:
The Court laid down the test for a fixed place PE: (a) existence of a physical location, (b) the foreign
enterprise's right to use that location, and (c) carrying out business through that location. The Court found that
FOWC had exclusive access to the circuit and complete control over the commercial exploitation of the event.
Even though the race lasted only three days, the nature of FOWC's business is touring. In the context of a
touring business, occupying a specific location exclusively for the duration of the event satisfies the test of
'permanence'. Since the PE existed, the income attributable to FOWC's commercial activities at the Indian track
was taxable in India.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. A 'Fixed Place Permanent Establishment' does not require ownership or year-round presence.
2. Absolute commercial and physical control over a location for the duration of an event can constitute a
PE, especially for touring businesses.
3. Income attributable to such a PE is fully taxable in the source country.

cases.title: DIT v. Morgan Stanley & Co. Inc.
cases.facts:
Morgan Stanley (a US company) established a captive BPO subsidiary in India (MSAS) to provide back-office
support services. Morgan Stanley sent some of its global executives to India on 'deputation' to manage and train
the staff at MSAS. The Revenue argued that by sending these executives, Morgan Stanley created a 'Service
Permanent Establishment' (Service PE) in India. Furthermore, the Revenue sought to attribute a portion of
Morgan Stanley's global profits to this Indian PE for taxation.
cases.issues:
1. Does deputing expatriate employees to an Indian subsidiary create a 'Service PE' for the foreign
parent company?
2. If a PE exists, but the Indian subsidiary is remunerated on an arm's-length basis, can further profits
be attributed to the foreign parent's PE?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
Morgan Stanley argued that the deputed employees worked entirely for the Indian subsidiary, not the US
parent. Therefore, no Service PE existed. Further, MSAS was paid at an arm's length price, extinguishing any
further tax liability.
B. Defendant / Revenue
The Revenue argued that the deputed employees remained on the payroll of the US parent, retaining their lien
on foreign employment. Thus, the US company was rendering services in India, creating a Service PE and
attracting tax on attributable profits.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court held that a Service PE existed, but ruled that no further profits could be attributed
to it since the subsidiary was paid at arm's length.
cases.reasoning:
The Court analyzed the deputation agreement. Since the expats retained a lien on their employment with the
US parent and the parent was ultimately responsible for their deployment, the US parent was deemed to be
providing services in India through its employees, thereby constituting a 'Service PE' under the DTAA.
However, the Court delivered a massive relief on the second issue. It held that the purpose of identifying a PE
is to tax the profits attributable to it. If the Indian subsidiary (which constitutes the PE) has already been
remunerated by the foreign parent on an 'arm's-length basis' (supported by a Transfer Pricing study), the
economic value of the PE's activity has been fully captured and taxed in India. No further profits can be
artificially attributed to the foreign parent.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Deputing employees to an Indian subsidiary while retaining control over their employment creates a
'Service PE'.
2. If the Indian entity (PE) is remunerated on an arm's-length basis, no further profits can be attributed to
the foreign enterprise.
3. Transfer pricing compliance acts as a shield against additional profit attribution to PEs.

cases.title: Mak Data P. Ltd. v. CIT
cases.facts:
During a search and seizure operation, certain incriminating documents were found indicating concealed
income. During the assessment proceedings, the assessee voluntarily surrendered a sum of Rs. 40.74 lakhs to
buy peace and avoid litigation, but explicitly stated that this surrender was conditional and should not be
construed as an admission of concealment. The Assessing Officer accepted the surrender, added it to the
income, and subsequently levied a heavy penalty under Section 271(1)(c) for 'concealment of income'.
cases.issues:
1. Does a voluntary surrender of income during assessment proceedings automatically absolve the
taxpayer from the penalty for concealment under Section 271(1)(c)?
2. Can an assessee place 'conditions' on a surrender to avoid penalties?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The assessee argued that the surrender was made voluntarily to buy peace. Since there was no formal finding or
definitive proof by the AO that the amount was actively concealed, penalty proceedings were unjustified.
B. Defendant / Revenue
The Revenue argued that the surrender was not voluntary; it was forced because the assessee was cornered by
the incriminating documents found during the search. Surrendering after being caught is an admission of
concealment.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Revenue, upholding the penalty and rejecting the defense of
'conditional surrender'.
cases.reasoning:
The Court took a strict stance on tax evasion. It held that the phrase 'voluntary surrender to buy peace' has no
legal standing in the Income Tax Act when incriminating evidence is discovered. An assessee cannot dictate
terms or place conditions on the Assessing Officer while surrendering income. The surrender was made only
after the assessee was confronted with evidence they could not explain. This is not a bona fide voluntary
disclosure but a forced admission. The Court ruled that the Assessing Officer is not required to find
independent, definitive proof of concealment if the assessee surrenders the income in the face of incriminating
documents. The penalty under Section 271(1)(c) was rightly levied.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Surrendering income to 'buy peace' does not automatically grant immunity from concealment penalties
under Section 271(1)(c).
2. A surrender made after the discovery of incriminating evidence is deemed an admission of
concealment.
3. Assessees cannot place legal conditions on the surrender of income to escape statutory penalties.

cases.title: Director of Income Tax v. E-Funds IT Solution Inc.
cases.facts:
E-Funds Inc. (a US company) established an Indian subsidiary (E-Funds India) to provide back-office BPO
services, primarily IT support and call center operations. E-Funds US assigned contracts to the Indian
subsidiary. The Revenue claimed that E-Funds US had a Permanent Establishment (PE) in India under three
grounds: a Fixed Place PE (because the US company used the Indian office), a Service PE (due to deputed
employees), and an Agency PE (because the Indian entity acted on its behalf).
cases.issues:
1. Does the mere outsourcing of back-office operations to a subsidiary in India create a Permanent
Establishment (PE) for the foreign parent?
2. What level of control is required to trigger a Fixed Place or Agency PE?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The Revenue argued that the Indian subsidiary was virtually a projection of the US company. The US company
provided the software, hardware guidelines, and clients, meaning the Indian premises were effectively at the
'disposal' of the US parent.
B. Defendant / Revenue
The assessee argued that outsourcing is a standard BPO model. The Indian subsidiary operated independently.
The US company did not have a 'right to use' the Indian premises, nor did the Indian company have the
authority to conclude contracts for the US parent.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the assessee, holding that outsourcing back-office operations does
not create a PE.
cases.reasoning:
The Court systematically rejected all three PE claims. First, a 'Fixed Place PE' requires the foreign enterprise to
have the physical premises at its 'disposal'. Merely giving software access or sending data for processing does
not give the US company control over the Indian premises. Second, a 'Service PE' requires deputed employees
to furnish services to third parties in India; here, they only supported the Indian subsidiary. Third, an 'Agency
PE' requires the Indian entity to habitually conclude binding contracts on behalf of the foreign parent. E-Funds
India merely processed data and had no authority to sign contracts. The Court firmly established that routine
IT/BPO outsourcing to India does not create a tax nexus for the foreign client.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Outsourcing back-office IT/BPO services to an Indian subsidiary does not inherently create a
Permanent Establishment (PE).
2. A Fixed Place PE requires the foreign entity to have the Indian premises at its physical 'disposal'.
3. An Agency PE requires the agent to have the authority to habitually conclude binding contracts for the
principal.

cases.title: CIT v. Bharti Cellular Ltd.
cases.facts:
Bharti Cellular (a telecom operator) sold pre-paid SIM cards and recharge vouchers to its distributors at a
discounted rate below the Maximum Retail Price (MRP). The distributors then sold them to retailers or end-
customers. The Income Tax Department argued that this 'discount' was essentially a 'commission' paid to the
distributors for acting as agents of Bharti Cellular. Consequently, the Department demanded that Bharti
Cellular should have deducted TDS on this discount under Section 194H (TDS on Commission or Brokerage).
cases.issues:
1. Is the relationship between a telecom operator and its SIM card distributor that of a 'Principal to
Principal' or 'Principal to Agent'?
2. Does the discount given on prepaid SIM cards constitute a 'commission' liable for TDS under Section
194H?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The Revenue argued that the distributors do not own the telecom services; they merely facilitate the connection
between the telecom company and the customer. Therefore, they act as agents, and the margin they retain is a
commission.
B. Defendant / Revenue
The assessee argued that the sale of SIM cards to distributors is on a 'principal-to-principal' basis. Once the
SIM cards are sold to the distributor, the property and risk pass to them. The difference between the MRP and
the sale price is a trade discount, not a commission.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court directed the tax authorities to establish the factual matrix of the specific contracts,
but laid down the foundational legal tests favoring the principal-to-principal argument.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that the applicability of Section 194H hinges entirely on the legal relationship established by
the franchise/distributorship agreement. If the agreement indicates that the distributor assumes the risk of loss,
pays for the SIM cards upfront, and has no right to return unsold cards, it points to a 'principal-to-principal'
transaction. A discount offered on a principal-to-principal sale is a reduction in the sale price, not a payment for
services rendered. Therefore, it does not qualify as 'commission' or 'brokerage' under Section 194H. The Court
remanded the cases to the assessing officers to examine the specific contracts to confirm if the risk actually
passed to the franchisees.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. TDS under Section 194H (Commission) applies only if a Principal-Agent relationship exists.
2. A trade discount given on a 'Principal-to-Principal' sale of goods (like SIM cards) is not a commission.
3. The passing of risk and ownership determines the nature of the relationship.

cases.title: Checkmate Services Pvt. Ltd. v. CIT
cases.facts:
The assessee company deducted the employees' share of Provident Fund (PF) and Employees' State Insurance
(ESI) contributions from their salaries. Under the respective labor laws, the employer must deposit these
collected amounts into the government funds by a strict monthly deadline. The assessee deposited the funds
after the labor law deadline, but before filing their Income Tax Return. The assessee claimed a deduction
for these amounts, relying on Section 43B of the ITA, which allows deductions if statutory dues are paid before
filing the tax return.
cases.issues:
1. Are employees' contributions to PF/ESI governed by Section 43B of the ITA?
2. Can an employer claim a deduction for employees' contributions if deposited after the labor law due
date, but before filing the income tax return?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The assessee argued that Section 43B (as amended) applies broadly to all statutory welfare payments. If the
money is paid before the tax return is filed, the deduction must be allowed to prevent undue hardship.
B. Defendant / Revenue
The Revenue argued that employees' contributions are fundamentally different from the employer's own
contributions. When an employer deducts money from an employee's salary, it becomes 'deemed income' of the
employer under Section 2(24)(x). It can only be deducted under Section 36(1)(va) if deposited precisely by the
strict due date under the PF Act. Section 43B does not apply.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Revenue, holding that late deposits of employees'
contributions cannot be claimed as deductions.
cases.reasoning:
The Court drew a strict, critical distinction between the employer's contribution and the employees'
contribution. The employer's own contribution is a business expense governed by Section 43B, which grants
the leniency of depositing it up to the tax return filing date. However, the employees' contribution is money
belonging to the employees that the employer holds in trust. Retaining this money is essentially
misappropriation. Therefore, Section 36(1)(va) creates a strict condition: this money is deemed income of the
employer and can only be deducted if deposited by the exact due date specified in the PF/ESI Acts. The
leniency of Section 43B absolutely does not apply to employees' contributions.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Employees' contributions to PF/ESI are distinct from the employer's contributions.
2. Section 43B (leniency till tax return filing date) applies only to the employer's own statutory
contributions.
3. Employees' contributions must be deposited by the strict labor law deadline; a delay results in
permanent disallowance of the deduction.

cases.title: Manish Maheshwari v. Asst. CIT
cases.facts:
A search and seizure operation (raid) was conducted under Section 132 of the ITA on the premises of a Director
of a company. During the search, some documents belonging to the assessee (Manish Maheshwari) were found.
Based on these documents, the Assessing Officer (AO) initiated block assessment proceedings against Manish
Maheshwari under Section 158BD. However, the AO of the Director (where the search happened) simply
forwarded the documents to Maheshwari's AO without recording any formal 'satisfaction' that the documents
indicated undisclosed income belonging to Maheshwari.
cases.issues:
1. What are the mandatory conditions precedent for initiating assessment proceedings against a third
party under Section 158BD (or Section 153C) based on documents found in someone else's search?
2. Is the recording of 'satisfaction' by the searching AO mandatory?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The assessee argued that the proceedings were void ab initio. Section 158BD explicitly requires the AO
conducting the search to be formally 'satisfied' that the seized documents belong to a third party and represent
undisclosed income before handing them over.
B. Defendant / Revenue
The Revenue argued that the transmission of the documents itself implied satisfaction. Procedural technicalities
shouldn't invalidate tax evasion proceedings.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the assessee, quashing the block assessment proceedings for
failing to follow the strict statutory procedure.
cases.reasoning:
The Court emphasized that search, seizure, and block assessments are draconian powers that encroach on a
citizen's privacy. Therefore, the statutory procedures must be strictly complied with. Section 158BD (and its
successor Section 153C) lays down a mandatory two-step process. First, the AO assessing the searched person
must examine the documents and record a formal 'satisfaction note' stating that the documents belong to a third
party (the assessee) and have a bearing on their income. Only after recording this satisfaction can the
documents be transmitted to the assessee's AO. Since this mandatory condition precedent was entirely
bypassed, the subsequent assessment against Manish Maheshwari lacked jurisdiction and was legally void.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. To assess a third party based on documents found in a search, the searching AO must record a
mandatory 'satisfaction note'.
2. The note must explicitly state that the documents belong to the third party and impact their taxable
income.
3. Failure to record this satisfaction renders the subsequent assessment proceedings against the third party
void ab initio.

cases.title: CIT v. Vegetable Products Ltd.
cases.facts:
The assessee filed its income tax return late. The Income Tax Officer levied a penalty under Section 271(1)(a)
of the ITA for the delayed filing. The penalty was to be calculated based on the 'tax payable on the income as
finally assessed'. However, the assessee had already paid a significant amount as provisional/advance tax
before the final assessment was completed. The dispute arose over the calculation of the penalty: should it be a
percentage of the total gross tax assessed, or only a percentage of the net tax remaining payable after deducting
the advance tax already paid?
cases.issues:
1. What is the interpretation of the phrase 'the amount of the tax, if any, payable by him' in penalty
provisions?
2. When there are two reasonable interpretations of a penal tax provision, which interpretation should
the court adopt?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The assessee argued that 'tax payable' means the actual amount of tax the assessee still owes the government
after adjusting advance taxes. Levying a penalty on the gross amount when the government already had the
money is unjust.
B. Defendant / Revenue
The Revenue argued a strict literal interpretation: 'tax payable' refers to the total tax liability determined upon
assessment, irrespective of what was paid in advance.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the assessee, establishing a foundational principle of interpreting
ambiguous tax statutes.
cases.reasoning:
The Court found that the statutory language 'the amount of the tax, if any, payable by him' was ambiguous and
capable of both interpretations. To resolve this, the Court laid down a cardinal rule of tax jurisprudence: if a
taxing provision (especially a penal provision) is ambiguous and capable of two reasonable interpretations, the
interpretation that is favorable to the assessee must be adopted. The Court reasoned that penalties are harsh, and
if the legislature leaves a loophole or ambiguity, the state cannot exploit it to extract a higher penalty.
Therefore, 'tax payable' was interpreted beneficially to mean the net tax outstanding after deducting the
advance tax paid.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. In case of ambiguity in a taxing or penal statute, the interpretation favorable to the assessee must be
adopted.
2. Penalties must be calculated strictly on the net outstanding tax liability, not the gross assessed tax, if
the language permits.
3. The burden of clear drafting in penal tax provisions lies on the legislature.

cases.title: Parashuram Pottery Works Co. Ltd. v. ITO
cases.facts:
Parashuram Pottery Works claimed initial depreciation on certain assets, which the Income Tax Officer allowed
during the original assessment. Many years later, the ITO realized he had made a mistake in law by allowing
that specific depreciation. Attempting to correct his own mistake, the ITO issued a notice to reopen the
assessment under Section 147 of the ITA. The assessee challenged this, arguing that the reopening was barred
by limitation and that they had fully disclosed all primary facts during the original assessment.
cases.issues:
1. Can an assessment be reopened beyond the statutory limitation period if the assessee fully disclosed all
facts originally?
2. What is the importance of finality in tax assessments?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The assessee argued that under Section 147, reopening beyond four years is only permissible if the income
escaped assessment due to the assessee's failure to disclose fully and truly all material facts. Since the mistake
was entirely the ITO's, the reopening was illegal.
B. Defendant / Revenue
The Revenue argued that the incorrect allowance of depreciation resulted in revenue loss, and the state must
have the power to rectify legal errors to collect the rightful tax.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the assessee, quashing the reassessment notice and emphasizing
the doctrine of finality.
cases.reasoning:
The Court strictly enforced the statutory conditions for reassessment. It confirmed that if the assessee has fully
and truly disclosed all material primary facts, the ITO cannot reopen the assessment beyond the limitation
period just because he later realizes he drew the wrong legal inference. Furthermore, the Court delivered a
philosophical ruling on the nature of tax litigation. It stated that there must be a point of finality in all legal
proceedings. Keeping taxpayers in perpetual suspense and allowing the sword of Damocles to hang over their
heads indefinitely based on the changing whims of assessing officers is oppressive and against the rule of law.
A stale claim cannot be resurrected merely because the tax officer made an error.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. An assessment cannot be reopened beyond the limitation period if the assessee made a full and true
disclosure of primary facts.
2. The Revenue cannot use Section 147 to correct its own subsequent legal realizations or change of
opinion.
3. The principle of finality is essential in tax laws to protect citizens from perpetual harassment.

cases.title: Godrej & Boyce Mfg. Co. Ltd. v. DCIT
cases.facts:
Godrej & Boyce earned substantial tax-free dividend income from its investments in shares. Section 14A of the
ITA disallows any expenditure incurred in relation to earning exempt income. Prior to 2008, Assessing Officers
estimated this disallowance subjectively. In 2008, the CBDT introduced Rule 8D, which prescribed a rigid
mathematical formula (a percentage of the average value of investments) to calculate the disallowance under
Section 14A. The Revenue attempted to apply this rigid Rule 8D formula retrospectively to the assessee's cases
from earlier assessment years (e.g., AY 2002-03).
cases.issues:
1. Does Rule 8D of the Income Tax Rules, which provides a mathematical formula for disallowance
under Section 14A, have retrospective application?
2. How should disallowance under Section 14A be calculated for years prior to the introduction of Rule
8D?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The assessee argued that Rule 8D created a new, substantive, and rigid liability mechanism. Substantive rules
cannot be applied retrospectively. For prior years, the AO must determine the disallowance on a reasonable
basis looking at actual facts, not a blind formula.
B. Defendant / Revenue
The Revenue argued that Rule 8D was merely procedural machinery created to calculate an already existing
liability under Section 14A. Procedural rules are inherently retrospective.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the assessee, holding that Rule 8D operates only prospectively
from Assessment Year 2008-09 onwards.
cases.reasoning:
The Court distinguished between the substantive law (Section 14A) and the machinery provision (Rule 8D).
Section 14A clearly applied retrospectively as it was a clarification of the law. However, Rule 8D introduced an
artificial mathematical formula that could result in disallowing amounts far exceeding the actual expenditure
incurred. Applying such a rigid, formulaic burden retrospectively would be harsh and unfair. The Court ruled
that Rule 8D is prospective. For assessment years prior to 2008-09, the Assessing Officer is duty-bound to
determine the disallowance on a 'reasonable basis' by examining the specific facts and accounts of the assessee,
rather than applying the mechanical formula of Rule 8D.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Rule 8D of the Income Tax Rules applies prospectively from Assessment Year 2008-09.
2. For prior years, disallowance under Section 14A must be calculated on a reasonable, factual basis, not a
mechanical formula.
3. Artificial tax computation formulas cannot be applied retrospectively unless explicitly mandated.

cases.title: South Indian Bank Ltd. v. CIT
cases.facts:
South Indian Bank had mixed funds-a common pool consisting of its own interest-free funds (share capital,
reserves) and interest-bearing borrowed funds. The bank made investments in tax-free bonds out of this
common pool. When computing the disallowance under Section 14A (expenditure incurred to earn exempt
income), the Revenue disallowed a proportionate amount of the interest paid on the borrowed funds, assuming
that the tax-free investments were made proportionately from both owned and borrowed funds.
cases.issues:
1. When an assessee has mixed funds (both interest-free and interest-bearing), and makes investments
yielding tax-free income, what is the legal presumption regarding the source of those investments?
2. Can the Revenue automatically apply a proportionate disallowance of interest under Section 14A?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The assessee bank argued that its own interest-free funds (reserves) far exceeded the value of the tax-free
investments. Under business principles, it must be presumed that the tax-free investments were made out of
their own interest-free funds, not the borrowed funds. Hence, no interest expenditure should be disallowed.
B. Defendant / Revenue
The Revenue argued that money is fungible. In a mixed pool, it is impossible to trace the exact source of a
specific investment. Therefore, a proportionate disallowance of interest is the only logical method.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the assessee, establishing a strong legal presumption regarding
the use of mixed funds.
cases.reasoning:
The Court established a highly beneficial rule for taxpayers. It held that where an assessee possesses a mixed
pool of funds, and the amount of their own interest-free funds (share capital, reserves, surplus) is sufficient to
cover the investments made in tax-free assets, a legal presumption arises in favor of the assessee. The law will
presume that the tax-free investments were made exclusively out of the assessee's own interest-free funds.
Consequently, no part of the interest paid on the borrowed funds can be linked to the exempt income, and no
disallowance can be made under Section 14A. The Revenue cannot force a proportionate disallowance if the
assessee's own funds exceed the investment.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. In cases of mixed funds, a legal presumption exists that investments yielding tax-free income were
made from the assessee's own interest-free funds.
2. This presumption holds true provided the assessee's own funds are equal to or greater than the tax-free
investments.
3. The Revenue cannot mechanically apply proportionate disallowance of interest under Section 14A
without tracing funds.

cases.title: Bangalore Club v. CIT
cases.facts:
Bangalore Club, a mutual association of members, deposited its surplus funds into fixed deposits in several
banks that were also corporate members of the club. The club earned interest on these fixed deposits. The club
argued that since the banks were members of the club, the interest earned from them should be exempt from
income tax under the 'Doctrine of Mutuality' (which exempts transactions between a club and its members).
cases.issues:
1. Does the Doctrine of Mutuality apply to interest earned on fixed deposits placed by a club with its
member banks?
2. What breaks the chain of mutuality in financial transactions?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The Club argued that since the borrower (the bank) was a member of the club, there was complete identity
between the contributor and the participator. Earning interest from a member is a mutual transaction.
B. Defendant / Revenue
The Revenue argued that the bank took the deposit not in its capacity as a club member enjoying a facility, but
in its capacity as a commercial banking institution. The funds were used by the bank for third-party commercial
lending, destroying the mutuality.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Revenue, holding that the interest earned on fixed deposits is
fully taxable business income, piercing the claim of mutuality.
cases.reasoning:
The Court reaffirmed the three tests of mutuality (identity of contributors/participators, instrumental purpose,
and impossibility of external profit). The Court held that when the club deposited money in the bank, the
mutuality was broken. The bank did not keep the money isolated for the club; it merged the funds with its
general commercial pool and loaned it out to third parties to earn commercial profits. The interest paid back to
the club was generated from transactions with these third-party outsiders. Because the chain of mutuality was
broken by the intervention of commercial third-party transactions, the interest income lacked the essential
'identity' requirement and was therefore taxable as 'Income from Other Sources'.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. The Doctrine of Mutuality does not apply to interest earned by a club on fixed deposits in member
banks.
2. The integration of club funds into a commercial banking pool used for third-party lending breaks the
chain of mutuality.
3. To claim mutuality, the surplus must be generated strictly from internal member transactions, not
commercial external exploitation.

cases.title: CIT v. Meghalaya Steels Ltd.
cases.facts:
To promote industrialization in backward areas (like the North-Eastern states), the Government provided
various subsidies to manufacturing units, including transport subsidies, interest subsidies, and power subsidies.
The assessee claimed a deduction under Section 80-IB of the ITA, which provides a tax holiday on profits
'derived from' an industrial undertaking. The Revenue excluded these subsidies from the calculation of the 80-
IB deduction, arguing that the subsidies were handouts from the government, not profits 'derived from' the
actual manufacturing activities of the business.
cases.issues:
1. Are transport, interest, and power subsidies considered profits 'derived from' an industrial
undertaking for the purpose of claiming a deduction under Section 80-IB?
2. What is the nexus required between the subsidy and the manufacturing activity?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The Revenue argued a strict 'first degree nexus' test. They contended that profits must flow directly from the
physical manufacturing and sale of goods. Subsidies are financial aid from the state, lacking a direct nexus to
the manufacturing process.
B. Defendant / Revenue
The assessee argued that the subsidies were specifically given to reimburse the inflated costs of transport,
power, and interest incurred because they set up a factory in a difficult geographical area. Thus, the subsidies
directly reduced their manufacturing costs, boosting their business profits.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the assessee, holding that such cost-reimbursement subsidies are
profits derived from the industrial undertaking.
cases.reasoning:
The Court distinguished between different types of subsidies. It held that the transport, power, and interest
subsidies in this case were not arbitrary grants. They were specifically designed to reimburse the manufacturer
for the extra expenses incurred in running an industry in a backward area. By reimbursing these specific
operational costs, the subsidies directly reduced the cost of production. A reduction in the cost of production
intrinsically increases the business profit. Therefore, there is a direct, first-degree nexus between the receipt of
these subsidies and the industrial operations. Consequently, these subsidies qualify as profits 'derived from' the
industrial undertaking and are eligible for the 100% deduction under Section 80-IB.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Subsidies that reimburse specific operational costs (transport, power) have a direct nexus with
manufacturing activities.
2. Such cost-reduction subsidies constitute profits 'derived from' the industrial undertaking.
3. They are fully eligible for tax holiday deductions under Section 80-IB.

cases.title: NDTV v. Deputy Commissioner of Income Tax
cases.facts:
New Delhi Television Ltd (NDTV) issued step-up coupon bonds through its UK subsidiary. Years after the
assessment was completed, the Income Tax Department issued a notice to reopen NDTV's assessment under
Section 147. However, the notice was issued beyond the standard 4-year limitation period. To justify reopening
after 4 years, the Revenue alleged that NDTV had failed to disclose the 'true nature' of the complex corporate
structure and the ultimate beneficiaries of the funds. The Revenue argued that since foreign assets were
involved, the extended limitation period of 16 years should apply.
cases.issues:
1. Can the Revenue invoke the extended 16-year limitation period for reassessment under Section 147
merely by alleging complex foreign transactions?
2. Does the failure to disclose 'secondary facts' justify reopening an assessment beyond 4 years?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The Revenue argued that the entire bond issuance was a sham transaction designed to round-trip black money.
Because it involved foreign entities and hidden ultimate beneficiaries, it fell under the extended limitation
provisions for foreign assets.
B. Defendant / Revenue
NDTV argued that it had disclosed all primary facts regarding the UK subsidiary, the bonds, and the investors
during the original assessment. The Revenue was trying to reopen the case purely on a 'change of opinion'
regarding facts they already had.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of NDTV on the primary disclosure issue, strictly limiting the
Revenue's power to reopen assessments beyond four years, but remanded the specific 'foreign asset' point for
factual verification.
cases.reasoning:
The Court strongly reiterated the Calcutta Discount principle. If an assessee has disclosed all primary facts
during the original assessment, the Revenue cannot reopen the case after four years simply because they want
to draw a different legal inference now. NDTV had fully disclosed the existence of its UK subsidiary and the
bond transaction. There was no 'failure to disclose material facts'. However, regarding the extended 16-year
limitation for 'foreign assets', the Court noted that if the Revenue can specifically prove that the assessee was
the ultimate beneficial owner of a hidden foreign asset, the 16-year limit applies. But the Revenue cannot use
this extended limit as a fishing expedition without concrete foundational evidence.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Reopening an assessment beyond 4 years requires proof that the assessee actively failed to disclose
primary facts.
2. A mere 'change of opinion' on previously disclosed facts makes reassessment illegal.
3. The extended 16-year limitation period for foreign assets requires tangible proof of hidden beneficial
ownership, not mere suspicion.

cases.title: CIT v. K. Raheja Development Corp.
cases.facts:
K. Raheja Development Corporation engaged in the business of constructing and selling residential apartments.
They entered into agreements with buyers where the buyers paid in installments as the construction progressed.
Upon completion, the physical possession and sale deed were transferred to the buyer. The Sales Tax
Department categorized these agreements as 'Works Contracts' and demanded sales tax. The developer argued
it was a pure sale of immovable real estate, not a works contract.
cases.issues:
1. Does an agreement to construct and sell an apartment, where payment is made in installments during
construction, constitute a 'Works Contract' liable to sales tax/V AT?
2. What is the distinction between a contract for sale of real estate and a works contract?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The developer argued that they were constructing the building on their own land. The agreement was to sell a
completed flat. Under Indian law, a contract for the sale of immovable property does not involve the 'sale of
goods' and is outside the purview of sales tax.
B. Defendant / Revenue
The Revenue argued that since the buyer was paying in installments during construction, the developer was
essentially building the flat for the buyer. Thus, it was a composite contract involving the supply of labor and
materials (a works contract).
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Revenue, classifying the construction agreements as 'Works
Contracts' subject to sales tax/V AT.
cases.reasoning:
The Court fundamentally altered real estate taxation. It held that if an agreement is entered into before the
construction of a flat is completed, and the buyer pays installments as the construction progresses, the
developer is effectively undertaking construction on behalf of the buyer. The developer is supplying materials
and labor to build something for a specific client. This satisfies the definition of a 'Works Contract' under
Article 366(29A)(b) of the Constitution. Therefore, the state government has the power to levy sales tax/V AT
on the 'goods' portion (cement, steel, etc.) used in the construction of that specific flat. (Note: This principle
was later affirmed and expanded in the landmark L&T 2014 judgment)..
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Agreements to construct and sell apartments entered into before completion are classified as 'Works
Contracts'.
2. Developers must pay Sales Tax/V AT on the value of goods used in the construction of such apartments.
3. A contract for the sale of a fully completed, ready-to-move-in apartment is a pure sale of real estate and
escapes works contract tax.

cases.title: Union of India v. U.A.E. Exchange Centre
cases.facts:
U.A.E. Exchange Centre, a company based in the UAE, set up a 'Liaison Office' in India with permission from
the Reserve Bank of India. The sole activity of this liaison office was to download data regarding remittances
from UAE NRIs and print/dispatch cheques to beneficiaries in India. The office did not charge any fee in India,
nor did it enter into any contracts. The Revenue sought to tax the company, arguing that the liaison office
constituted a Permanent Establishment (PE) in India under the India-UAE DTAA, carrying out core business
activities.
cases.issues:
1. Does a Liaison Office performing back-office, preparatory, or auxiliary tasks constitute a Permanent
Establishment (PE) under a DTAA?
2. Are the activities of downloading data and printing cheques considered 'core business activities'?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The Revenue argued that transferring money was the core business of the exchange center. The Indian liaison
office completed the final, crucial step of the transaction (delivering the money). Therefore, it was heavily
involved in the core business, triggering a PE.
B. Defendant / Revenue
The assessee argued that Article 5(3)(e) of the DTAA explicitly excludes fixed places of business maintained
solely for carrying on activities of a 'preparatory or auxiliary character'. The contracts were signed and fees
collected entirely in the UAE.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the assessee, holding that the Liaison Office did not constitute a
Permanent Establishment.
cases.reasoning:
The Court strictly interpreted the exceptions within the DTAA. It held that to constitute a PE, the fixed place
must be engaged in core income-generating activities. The Court observed that the RBI explicitly restricts
liaison offices from earning any income or engaging in commercial/trading activities in India. The activities of
the Indian office-downloading data, printing cheques, and mailing them-were purely administrative,
supportive, and auxiliary in nature. The actual contract of remittance and the earning of the commission
happened entirely in the UAE. Since the Indian activities fell squarely within the 'preparatory or auxiliary
character' exception of the DTAA, the liaison office was not a PE, and its operations were completely immune
from Indian taxation.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. A Liaison Office engaging solely in administrative, preparatory, or auxiliary activities does not
constitute a Permanent Establishment.
2. Downloading data and dispatching cheques on behalf of a foreign parent are auxiliary tasks, not core
income-generating activities.
3. Compliance with RBI restrictions on liaison offices strongly supports the claim against the existence of
a PE.

cases.title: CIT v. Virtual Soft Systems Ltd.
cases.facts:
Virtual Soft Systems was engaged in the business of leasing machinery and equipment. The company claimed a
deduction for depreciation on the leased assets under Section 32 of the ITA. However, the lease agreements
were structured closely to 'Hire-Purchase' agreements. In a hire-purchase, the hirer ultimately has the option to
buy the asset. The Revenue disallowed the depreciation to the leasing company, arguing that in a hire-purchase
arrangement, the hirer (the customer) is the effective owner, and only the owner can claim depreciation.
cases.issues:
1. What is the distinction between a true 'lease' and a 'hire-purchase' agreement for tax purposes?
2. Can a lessor claim depreciation if the contract is fundamentally a hire-purchase agreement?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The assessee argued that the contract was titled a 'lease agreement'. As the lessor, they retained legal title to the
assets throughout the lease period and were therefore the 'owners' entitled to depreciation.
B. Defendant / Revenue
The Revenue argued that courts must look at the substance of the contract, not just the title. The agreement
gave the hirer the option to purchase the asset at a nominal price at the end, shifting the economic ownership
and risk to the hirer.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Revenue, holding that the contracts were hire-purchase
agreements, denying depreciation to the lessor.
cases.reasoning:
The Court emphasized the 'substance over form' doctrine in commercial contracts. A true lease involves merely
renting an asset without transferring ownership risks. A hire-purchase agreement is essentially a financing
arrangement to facilitate the ultimate purchase of the asset by the hirer. The Court analyzed the specific clauses
of the agreement and found that the entire cost of the asset plus interest was recovered during the 'lease' period,
and the hirer had an exclusive option to buy it for a token amount at the end. The real economic owner was the
hirer, not the finance company. Following the CBDT circulars and accounting standards on hire-purchase, the
Court held that the lessor is merely a financier and cannot claim depreciation; only the hirer (the real owner)
can.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. The 'substance over form' doctrine determines the true nature of a commercial contract in tax law.
2. In a hire-purchase agreement, the hirer (not the financier/lessor) is considered the owner for claiming
depreciation.
3. Contracts disguised as leases to claim tax benefits will be struck down if their economic reality is hire-
purchase.

cases.title: Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal
cases.facts:
The Finance Act 2021 introduced a new regime for reopening tax assessments (Section 148A),
mandating an inquiry and a show-cause notice before issuing a reassessment notice under
Section 148. However , due to COVID-19 delays, the government had passed the Taxation and
Other Laws (Relaxation) Act (TOLA), extending deadlines. Relying on TOLA, the Revenue
issued thousands of reassessment notices after April 1, 2021, using the 'old' procedure instead
of the newly enacted Section 148A. Multiple High Courts quashed these notices as legally
invalid.
cases.issues:
1. Could the Revenue use the old reassessment procedure after the new Section 148A
came into force on April 1, 2021, relying on TOLA extensions?
2. Should thousands of potentially valid tax demands be completely quashed due to an
administrative procedural error?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The assessees argued that once the old law was substituted by the Finance Act 2021, it ceased
to exist. Notices issued under a dead law are void ab initio. TOLA could only extend timelines,
not breathe life into repealed procedures.
B. Defendant / Revenue / State
The Revenue argued that they acted under the bona fide belief that TOLA saved the old
provisions due to the pandemic. Quashing 90,000 notices would cause massive revenue loss to
the exchequer .
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court invoked Article 142 to save the notices, converting the invalid
Section 148 notices into show-cause notices under the new Section 148A(b).
cases.reasoning:
The Court agreed with the High Courts that the Revenue made a legal error; the new law was
mandatory from April 1, 2021. However , the Court noted that the error was driven by genuine
confusion over the interplay between TOLA and the Finance Act. To balance the scales-
protecting the public exchequer from massive losses while safeguarding the new statutory
rights of the taxpayers-the Court used its extraordinary constitutional powers. It directed
that all the quashed notices be deemed as show-cause notices issued under the new Section
148A(b). The Revenue was directed to supply the underlying materials to the taxpayers,
giving them a chance to reply under the new, fairer regime.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Procedural tax laws amended to provide fairer processes to taxpayers must be strictly
followed from their effective date.
2. Article 142 can be invoked to correct massive administrative errors in tax litigation to
prevent systemic collapse.
3. Defective reassessment notices can be converted into show-cause notices to cure
procedural defects while saving the revenue.

cases.title: Pr . CIT v. Wipro Ltd.
cases.facts:
Wipro Ltd. initially filed its income tax return claiming a tax exemption for its 100% Export
Oriented Unit under Section 10B. Later , the company realized it had incurred a loss and
would rather carry forward the loss to future years than claim the exemption. To effect this
change, Wipro filed a simple letter with the Assessing Officer during the assessment
proceedings withdrawing its Section 10B claim. The AO rejected the letter , stating that such a
change could only be made by filing a formally 'Revised Return' under Section 139(5) within
the statutory deadline.
cases.issues:
1. Can an assessee alter a substantive claim (like withdrawing an exemption to carry
forward a loss) by simply filing a letter during assessment proceedings?
2. Is the filing of a revised return under Section 139(5) a mandatory statutory
requirement for altering claims?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The Revenue argued that the Income Tax Act is a self-contained code. Section 139(5)
specifically provides the mechanism to correct omissions or wrong statements. Allowing
changes via simple letters bypasses statutory deadlines and procedures.
B. Defendant / Revenue / State
The assessee argued that the purpose of assessment is to determine the correct tax liability. A
letter filed before the assessment is finalized should be accepted by the AO to ensure the
taxpayer isn't denied legitimate benefits due to procedural technicalities.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Revenue, holding that filing a revised return
under Section 139(5) is mandatory.
cases.reasoning:
The Court strictly interpreted the procedural mandates of the Income Tax Act. It held that
while an assessee has the right to withdraw a claim for exemption and opt to carry forward a
loss, the method of doing so is strictly governed by the statute. Section 139(5) allows an
assessee to file a revised return within a specific time frame to correct any omission. The
Court ruled that an Assessing Officer has no power to entertain fresh claims or the
withdrawal of substantive claims made through mere letters or revised computations during
the assessment. If the statutory deadline to file a revised return has passed, the original
return stands, and the new claim is legally invalid.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Substantive changes to a tax return can only be made by filing a 'Revised Return'
under Section 139(5).
2. Assessing Officers cannot entertain fresh claims or withdrawals made via ordinary
letters during assessment.
3. Strict compliance with statutory timelines and procedures is mandatory in tax law.

cases.title: Taparia Tools Ltd. v. Joint CIT
cases.facts:
Taparia Tools issued non-convertible debentures to investors. The company gave investors
two options: receive regular interest over the 5-year term, or receive a one-time, discounted
upfront payment of the entire 5-year interest immediately upon subscription. For the
investors who chose the upfront payment, the company physically paid out the money in Year
1. In its tax return, the company claimed the entire upfront interest paid as a deductible
business expenditure in Year 1. The Revenue disallowed this, arguing the expense should be
amortized (spread out) over the 5-year life of the debentures, as done in the company's own
accounting books.
cases.issues:
1. Can a taxpayer claim a full tax deduction in the first year for an upfront interest
payment that covers a multi-year liability?
2. Does the accounting treatment of an expense (amortization) dictate its tax
deductibility?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The assessee argued that under Section 36(1)(iii), a deduction is allowed for the amount of
interest 'paid' in respect of capital borrowed. Since the money actually left their bank account
in Year 1, the liability crystallized and was discharged, making it fully deductible in that year .
B. Defendant / Revenue / State
The Revenue argued the 'matching concept'. The borrowed funds would generate revenue
over 5 years, so the interest expense must be matched against that revenue over 5 years. This
was also how the company presented it to its shareholders.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the assessee, allowing the full deduction in the
year of actual payment.
cases.reasoning:
The Court firmly established that while accounting standards are relevant, they do not
override the express provisions of the Income Tax Act. Section 36(1)(iii) allows a deduction
for interest 'paid'. The Court noted that the company had actually discharged its liability by
paying the upfront discounted interest to the debenture holders. The liability had crystallized
definitively in Year 1. There was no deferred liability. Therefore, under the mercantile or cash
system, the expense was incurred. The fact that the company chose to amortize the expense
in its financial books to present a better profit picture to shareholders does not strip them of
their statutory right to claim the entire deduction in tax law in the year it was actually paid.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Upfront, one-time payment of multi-year interest is fully deductible in the year of
payment under Section 36(1)(iii).
2. The accounting treatment of an expense (like amortization) does not dictate its tax
deductibility.
3. Tax deductions rely on the actual crystallization and discharge of the legal liability.

cases.title: CIT v. Max India Ltd.
cases.facts:
The Assessing Officer (AO) passed an assessment order allowing a certain deduction. Years
later , a new interpretation of the law emerged from a High Court judgment suggesting the
deduction might have been incorrect. The AO invoked Section 154 of the Income Tax Act,
which allows the rectification of a 'mistake apparent from the record', to withdraw the
deduction and demand more tax. The assessee challenged this, arguing that Section 154
cannot be used for debatable issues.
cases.issues:
1. What is the precise scope of a 'mistake apparent from the record' under Section 154 of
the ITA?
2. Can an Assessing Officer use Section 154 to rectify an issue that involves a debatable
point of law or where two interpretations are possible?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The assessee argued that the original assessment was based on a perfectly valid legal
interpretation at the time. Section 154 is for glaring clerical or arithmetic errors, not for
revising legal opinions.
B. Defendant / Revenue / State
The Revenue argued that the subsequent High Court judgment proved the original order was
legally wrong, making the error apparent from the record and rectifiable.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the assessee, quashing the rectification order
under Section 154.
cases.reasoning:
The Court laid down the definitive test for Section 154. A 'mistake apparent from the record'
must be an obvious, glaring, and patent mistake. It must not be a mistake that requires a long,
drawn-out process of reasoning or legal argument to discover . Crucially, the Court held that if
a legal issue is debatable, or if two reasonable legal views are possible on the same subject, it
completely falls outside the scope of Section 154. The AO cannot use the rectification
provision as a disguised mechanism to review their own orders or apply new legal
interpretations. Such complex legal errors must be corrected through the appellate process or
reassessment (Section 147), not rectification.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Section 154 (Rectification) is strictly limited to glaring, obvious, and patent errors.
2. If a point of law is debatable or capable of two interpretations, it is NOT a 'mistake
apparent from the record'.
3. Rectification cannot be used as a substitute for a legal review or appeal.

cases.title: Shiv Raj Gupta v. CIT
cases.facts:
The assessee sold his controlling shares in a liquor company to a rival business. Along with
the share transfer agreement, the assessee entered into a separate 'Non-Compete Agreement',
under which he was paid a massive sum of money (Non-Compete Fee) in exchange for
promising not to start a competing liquor business for the next ten years. The transaction
occurred in 1994. The Revenue sought to tax this non-compete fee as business income or
capital gains. The assessee argued it was a 'capital receipt' entirely immune from taxation
under the law as it stood in 1994.
cases.issues:
1. Is a Non-Compete Fee received for not carrying on a business treated as a taxable
revenue receipt or a non-taxable capital receipt (prior to the 2003 amendment)?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The assessee argued that giving up the right to run a business is surrendering a capital asset
(the right to trade). Compensation for the sterilization of a capital asset is a capital receipt,
which was not taxable before specific laws were enacted.
B. Defendant / Revenue / State
The Revenue argued that the non-compete agreement was a sham; it was simply a colorable
device to inflate the sale price of the shares while disguising the premium as a non-taxable
receipt.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the assessee, holding the non-compete fee was a
non-taxable capital receipt.
cases.reasoning:
The Court clarified the historical tax treatment of non-compete fees. Prior to April 1, 2003
(when Section 28(va) was explicitly inserted into the ITA to tax non-compete fees as business
income), the law was clear: a payment received for agreeing not to carry on a business
relates to the sterilization of the very source of income. It is a loss of a capital asset (the right
to trade). Therefore, it constitutes a capital receipt. Because it lacked a 'cost of acquisition', it
also escaped capital gains tax under the B.C. Srinivasa Setty principle. Regarding the 'sham'
argument, the Court held that the Revenue failed to prove the agreement was fake. The buyer
legitimately paid the premium to eliminate a powerful competitor .
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Prior to the insertion of Section 28(va) in 2003, a Non-Compete Fee was a capital
receipt, not taxable as business income.
2. Compensation for the sterilization of a right to trade is a capital receipt.
3. The Revenue must have concrete proof to classify a distinct commercial agreement as
a sham.

cases.title: Assistant Commissioner of State Tax v. Commercial Steel Limited
cases.facts:
A truck carrying goods belonging to Commercial Steel Limited was intercepted by GST
authorities. Finding discrepancies in the e-way bill, the authorities detained the goods and
issued notices under the GST Act demanding tax and penalties. Instead of filing an appeal
before the statutory Appellate Authority under the GST Act, the company directly filed a Writ
Petition in the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution, asking the Court to quash the
detention orders. The High Court entertained the writ and ruled in favor of the company. The
State appealed to the Supreme Court.
cases.issues:
1. Should High Courts entertain writ petitions under Article 226 when a comprehensive
statutory appellate remedy is available under the GST Act?
2. What are the specific exceptions allowing a writ petition to bypass statutory tax
remedies?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The State argued that the GST Act provides a complete, self-contained mechanism for appeals.
High Courts usurping this role disrupts the uniform application of the law and clogs
constitutional courts with routine tax disputes.
B. Defendant / Revenue / State
The assessee argued that the detention was arbitrary and illegal, justifying the immediate
intervention of the High Court to protect their fundamental right to trade.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the State, severely reprimanding the High Court
for bypassing the statutory GST appellate mechanism.
cases.reasoning:
The Court laid down strict boundaries for writ jurisdictions in tax matters. It held that when a
statute creates a specific right and provides a dedicated appellate machinery to enforce that
right (like the GST Act), High Courts must not entertain writ petitions under Article 226. The
exhaustion of statutory remedies is the general rule. The Court outlined only three narrow
exceptions where a writ is permissible: (1) if there is a breach of fundamental rights, (2) if the
order is passed with a complete lack of jurisdiction (e.g., by the wrong officer), or (3) if the
principles of natural justice are blatantly violated. Since none of these exceptions applied
here, the High Court erred in entertaining the writ.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. High Courts must not entertain Article 226 writ petitions in tax disputes if an effective
statutory appellate remedy exists.
2. The GST Act is a self-contained code; its appellate hierarchy must be respected.
3. Writ jurisdiction is reserved for breaches of natural justice, lack of jurisdiction, or
violation of fundamental rights.

cases.title: Union of India v. Bombay Tyre International Ltd.
cases.facts:
Manufacturers of various goods challenged the method used by the Central Excise
Department to calculate 'Assessable Value' for levying excise duty. The manufacturers argued
that excise duty is a tax on 'manufacture'. Therefore, the assessable value should strictly be
the actual manufacturing cost plus manufacturing profit. They argued that any post-
manufacturing expenses-such as outward freight (transportation), advertising, marketing,
and special packaging-must be entirely excluded from the value before levying the tax.
cases.issues:
1. What constitutes the 'Assessable Value' for levying Central Excise duty?
2. Should post-manufacturing expenses like packaging, advertising, and outward freight
be included in or excluded from the assessable value?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The manufacturers argued that including marketing and freight artificially inflates the
'manufacturing' tax into a sales tax. Advertising and transport happen after the goods are
fully manufactured.
B. Defendant / Revenue / State
The Revenue argued that the wholesale price at the factory gate is the correct assessable
value. Goods are only marketable when packaged and advertised, so these costs are integral
to the wholesale price.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: A Constitution Bench delivered a landmark judgment defining 'Assessable Value',
ruling partly for the Revenue and partly for the assessees.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that Central Excise is indeed a tax on manufacture, but it is collected at the
point of sale (the factory gate). Therefore, the 'wholesale cash price' at the factory gate is the
legally valid assessable value. The Court clarified the inclusion of specific costs: (1) Packaging:
All costs of primary and secondary packing necessary to make the goods marketable at the
factory gate must be INCLUDED in the value. (2) Advertising/Marketing: These build the brand
and demand before the sale at the factory gate, so they are INCLUDED. (3) Outward Freight/
Insurance: The cost of transporting goods from the factory gate to the buyer's destination
occurs after the clearance. Therefore, freight and transit insurance are true post-
manufacturing expenses and must be EXCLUDED from the assessable value.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Excise Assessable Value is the wholesale cash price at the factory gate.
2. Costs of packaging and advertising are integral to making goods marketable and are
included in the assessable value.
3. Outward freight and transit insurance are true post-manufacturing expenses and are
strictly excluded from excise valuation.

cases.title: Assistant CIT v. Hotel Blue Moon
cases.facts:
The Income Tax Department conducted a search and seizure operation on Hotel Blue Moon.
Under the special provisions for block assessments (Chapter XIV-B), the Assessing Officer (AO)
is required to issue a notice under Section 143(2) before finalizing the assessment, giving the
assessee an opportunity to present their case. The AO failed to issue this mandatory Section
143(2) notice and proceeded to pass the block assessment order demanding massive taxes
and penalties. The assessee challenged the assessment as legally void.
cases.issues:
1. Is the issuance of a notice under Section 143(2) a mandatory procedural requirement
in Block Assessment proceedings?
2. Does the failure to issue this notice render the entire assessment order void, or is it a
curable defect?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The assessee argued that Section 143(2) embodies the fundamental principle of natural
justice. Skipping this statutory notice deprives the taxpayer of the right to be heard, stripping
the AO of jurisdiction to pass the final order .
B. Defendant / Revenue / State
The Revenue argued that block assessments follow a special procedure under Section 158BC.
The failure to issue a 143(2) notice was merely a procedural irregularity, not a fatal
jurisdictional defect, especially since the assessee was aware of the search.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the assessee, declaring the block assessment
order completely void.
cases.reasoning:
The Court strictly interpreted the statutory procedure. It held that the provisions of Chapter
XIV-B (block assessments) must be read in harmony with the regular assessment procedures.
The issuance of a notice under Section 143(2) is not a mere procedural formality; it is a
mandatory, substantive requirement. It is the very mechanism through which the AO
assumes jurisdiction to scrutinize the return and make additions to the income. If an AO
wants to reject the income declared by the assessee and assess it at a higher figure, they are
legally bound to issue the 143(2) notice within the prescribed time limit. The omission to do so
is a fatal jurisdictional flaw that cannot be cured, rendering the entire block assessment void
ab initio.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. The issuance of a notice under Section 143(2) is a mandatory condition precedent for
completing a block assessment.
2. It is a jurisdictional requirement, not a curable procedural irregularity.
3. Failure to issue the notice within the statutory time limit renders the entire assessment
order legally void.

cases.title: Radhasoami Satsang v. CIT
cases.facts:
Radhasoami Satsang is a religious and charitable trust. For over three decades, the Income
Tax Department had recognized its charitable status and granted it tax exemption under
Sections 11 and 12 of the ITA. Suddenly, for a specific assessment year , a new Assessing Officer
decided to deny the exemption, arguing that the trust's income was being used for non-
charitable purposes. The facts, the trust deed, and the activities of the trust had not changed
at all from the previous decades.
cases.issues:
1. Does the principle of res judicata apply to income tax proceedings?
2. Can the Revenue abruptly deny a tax exemption that has been consistently granted
for decades, when the underlying facts remain completely unchanged?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The assessee argued that while each assessment year is separate, the Revenue cannot
arbitrarily flip-flop. The principle of consistency demands that settled legal positions based on
identical facts should not be disturbed by new officers.
B. Defendant / Revenue / State
The Revenue argued the strict legal doctrine that res judicata (a matter already judged)
does not apply in tax laws. Every assessment year is a fresh, independent proceeding, and an
AO is free to take a new legal view.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the trust, enforcing the 'Principle of Consistency'
in tax administration.
cases.reasoning:
The Court acknowledged the fundamental rule that res judicata does not strictly apply to
income tax proceedings, because the tax liability for each year is independent. However , the
Court carved out a massive, pragmatic exception based on fairness. It held that where a
fundamental aspect permeating through different assessment years has been settled and
accepted by the Revenue over a long period, and the underlying facts or law have not
changed, it would be unjust and unreasonable to allow a new Assessing Officer to arbitrarily
take a different view. The 'Principle of Consistency' must prevail to prevent taxpayer
harassment. Since the trust's structure and operations were identical to the past 30 years, the
exemption could not be suddenly withdrawn.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. While strict res judicata does not apply to tax proceedings, the 'Principle of
Consistency' must be respected.
2. The Revenue cannot arbitrarily change its stance on a settled issue in a subsequent
year if the facts and law remain identical.
3. Long-standing tax exemptions cannot be withdrawn merely due to a new officer's
change of opinion.

cases.title: Japan Airlines Co Ltd v. CIT
cases.facts:
Japan Airlines and other international carriers paid 'landing and parking charges' to the
Airports Authority of India (AAI) for using Indian airports. The airlines deducted TDS under
Section 194C (at 2%), treating the payment as a contract for 'work' or services (maintenance of
runways, air traffic control). The Income Tax Department argued the deduction was wrong.
They claimed the airlines were 'renting' the land (the runway and parking bays) and should
have deducted TDS under Section 194-I (Rent) at the much higher rate of 20%.
cases.issues:
1. Do landing and parking charges paid by airlines constitute 'Rent' for the use of land
(Section 194-I) or payment for carrying out 'Work/Services' (Section 194C)?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The airlines argued that landing an aircraft requires a highly sophisticated suite of services-
air traffic control, navigation aids, fire safety, and runway maintenance. They are paying for
these composite services, not 'leasing' a strip of tarmac.
B. Defendant / Revenue / State
The Revenue argued a literal interpretation of Section 194-I, which defines rent as any
payment for the use of any land or building. Since the aircraft physically touches and rests on
AAI land, the payment is rent.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the airlines, holding that the charges fall under
Section 194C (Work/Services), not Section 194-I (Rent).
cases.reasoning:
The Court analyzed the substance of the transaction. It held that when an airline pays landing
charges, it is not merely renting a piece of land to park a vehicle. The payment is for a
complex array of essential, highly technical services provided by the airport authority,
without which landing would be impossible (navigational facilities, security, runway
maintenance). The use of the land (the runway) is entirely incidental to the provision of these
comprehensive services. To classify these sophisticated aviation services as mere 'rent' is a
gross mischaracterization of the economic reality. Therefore, the payments constituted a
contract for services, correctly attracting TDS under Section 194C.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Landing and parking charges paid to airports are for composite technical services, not
for the mere use of land.
2. Such payments attract TDS under Section 194C (Contracts) and not under Section 194-I
(Rent).
3. If the use of land is purely incidental to a broader service contract, it does not
constitute a lease or rental agreement.

cases.title: UCO Bank v. CIT
cases.facts:
UCO Bank had advanced loans that had become 'sticky' (doubtful of recovery). Following a
circular issued by the Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT), the bank credited the interest on
these doubtful loans to a 'Suspense Account' instead of its main Profit & Loss account. The
CBDT circular specifically allowed banks not to pay tax on this interest until it was actually
realized. Later , the Assessing Officer ignored the CBDT circular , arguing it was contrary to the
mercantile system of accounting embedded in the Income Tax Act, and sought to tax the
interest on an accrual basis.
cases.issues:
1. Are Circulars issued by the Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) under Section 119
binding on the Income Tax authorities?
2. Can a CBDT circular be enforced even if it appears to deviate from the strict literal
text of the Income Tax Act, provided it is beneficial to the assessee?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The assessee bank argued that CBDT circulars are statutory directions. Tax officers are legally
bound to follow them. They structured their accounts relying on the explicit relief provided
by the Board.
B. Defendant / Revenue / State
The Revenue argued that the CBDT cannot issue circulars that contradict the parent statute.
Since the Act mandates taxing mercantile accruals, a circular granting an exemption is ultra
vires and can be ignored by an Assessing Officer .
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the assessee, cementing the binding nature of
CBDT circulars on tax authorities.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that Section 119 of the ITA grants the CBDT wide administrative powers to
issue orders, instructions, and circulars for the proper administration of the Act. The Court
unequivocally declared that these circulars are strictly binding on all income tax authorities.
Crucially, the Court held that the CBDT has the power to issue circulars that tone down the
rigor of the law or grant administrative relief to taxpayers in complex situations (like sticky
loans). Even if a circular deviates slightly from the strict letter of the law, if it is beneficial to
the assessee, the Revenue authorities cannot repudiate it. The department cannot take a
stance contrary to its own Board's beneficial directives.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. CBDT Circulars issued under Section 119 are legally binding on all Income Tax
authorities.
2. Tax authorities cannot ignore or challenge a circular that grants a benefit or relief to
the taxpayer .
3. The CBDT has the power to tone down the strict rigor of the statute to ensure practical
and fair tax administration.

cases.title: CIT v. Piara Singh
cases.facts:
Piara Singh was engaged in the illegal business of smuggling currency across the Indo-
Pakistan border . The Indian police and customs authorities caught him, and his smuggled
currency was confiscated by the state. The Income Tax Department sought to tax the profits
he made from his smuggling activities. Piara Singh argued that if his illegal income is being
taxed, then the confiscation of his currency by the authorities was a risk inherent to his
business, and he should be allowed to claim the confiscated amount as a deductible 'business
loss' under Section 37.
cases.issues:
1. Is income derived from an illegal business taxable under the Income Tax Act?
2. If illegal income is taxed, can the assessee claim a deduction for losses (like
confiscation by authorities) that are intrinsic to that illegal business?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The assessee argued that the Income Tax Act is color-blind; it taxes income whether from
legal or illegal sources. Therefore, the computation of that income must also be color-blind,
allowing all commercial losses directly connected to the trade.
B. Defendant / Revenue / State
The Revenue argued that allowing a deduction for confiscated smuggled goods would be
against public policy, as it essentially subsidizes criminal activity and softens the blow of a
penal confiscation.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the assessee, allowing the deduction for the
confiscated currency as a business loss.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a highly logical, albeit controversial, ruling on the symmetry of taxation.
It reaffirmed that the Income Tax Act does not distinguish between legal and illegal
businesses; tainted money is fully taxable. However , the Court held that if the State chooses to
tax the profits of an illegal business, it must assess the true commercial profits. In the
business of smuggling, the risk of getting caught and having goods confiscated by customs is a
direct, intrinsic, and foreseeable commercial risk. It is a loss that springs directly from the
carrying on of that specific trade. Therefore, to compute the true income of the smuggling
business, the confiscation loss must be allowed as a deduction. The State cannot tax the gross
receipts of a crime while ignoring the costs inherent in committing it.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Income from illegal businesses (like smuggling) is fully taxable under the Income Tax
Act.
2. When taxing an illegal business, losses directly intrinsic to that trade (like confiscation
of contraband) are deductible as business losses.
3. The computation of income must reflect the true commercial reality of the specific
trade, regardless of its legality.

cases.title: CIT v. Calcutta Knitwears
cases.facts:
A search was conducted on a person under Section 132. The Assessing Officer (AO) of the
searched person found documents relating to a third party (Calcutta Knitwears). The AO
handed over these documents to the AO of the third party. However , the searching AO failed
to record a formal 'satisfaction note' at the time of the search or during the assessment of the
searched person. The satisfaction note was recorded much later , after the documents were
already sent. The assessee challenged the block assessment proceedings under Section 158BD.
cases.issues:
1. At what exact stage must the Assessing Officer of the searched person record the
mandatory 'satisfaction note' to validly initiate proceedings against a third party under
Section 158BD?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Assessee
The assessee argued that the jurisdiction to assess a third party only triggers if the satisfaction
note is recorded before the documents are transmitted. A belated, back-dated note is a fatal
jurisdictional error .
B. Defendant / Revenue / State
The Revenue argued that the statute does not prescribe a rigid timeline for recording
satisfaction. As long as it is recorded before the third party's assessment is finalized, it cures
the procedural defect.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the assessee, establishing a strict timeline for
recording the satisfaction note, invalidating the delayed action.
cases.reasoning:
Building on the Manish Maheshwari precedent, the Court clarified the precise
chronological sequence required by Section 158BD (and Sec 153C). The Court held that the
recording of satisfaction by the searching AO is the absolute jurisdictional bedrock for third-
party assessments. This satisfaction must be recorded at one of three specific stages: (a) at the
time of initiating the assessment of the searched person, (b) during the course of their
assessment, or (c) immediately after the completion of their assessment, but strictly before
the documents are transmitted to the AO of the third party. Once the documents are handed
over without a note, the searching AO becomes functus officio (loses authority) regarding
those documents. A post-facto satisfaction note is invalid and cannot retroactively cure the
jurisdictional void.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. The 'satisfaction note' for third-party assessments (Sec 158BD/153C) must be recorded
by the searching AO.
2. It must be recorded before the seized documents are transmitted to the third party's
AO.
3. A belated satisfaction note renders the entire third-party assessment legally void.

cases.title: Padmini Products v. Collector of Central Excise
cases.facts:
Padmini Products manufactured agarbattis (incense sticks). Under a long-standing practice
and belief that their specific type of agarbatti was exempt from excise duty, they did not pay
duty or declare it in their filings. The Excise Department suddenly decided the goods were
